author: henry
old: First letter in the collection. Documents the 34th NY's journey from Albany to Washington in the opening weeks of the war, including passage through Baltimore — a city where a riot had killed soldiers just weeks earlier (April 19, 1861).
final: Henry's first letter home: the 34th New York reaches Washington after a river boat from Albany and a half-mile march through Baltimore, where twenty of his company carried loaded guns "in case of attack" but the city "rather cheered" them. In the depot he counts bullet holes from an earlier row and sees a volunteer accidentally killed by a dropped gun. Mindful of his widowed mother, he declines a costly furlough, trusting she needs the eight dollars he sent more than he needs the visit.

author: henry
old: Henry is writing from Washington while hearing the cannons of the First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) — the first major battle of the Civil War, fought July 21, 1861, approximately 25-30 miles from Washington. This is a real-time eyewitness account of the battle's sound reaching the capital.
final: Writing from Washington on July 21, 1861, Henry tells his mother that "while I am writing there is a battle going on," with cannons firing "not over twenty-eight miles from here" — a Union soldier's real-time account of First Bull Run reaching the capital by sound alone. He doesn't yet know whether his regiment will march or hold as city guard, and steadies himself in faith hours after a six o'clock chapel service: wherever he goes, he is ready.

author: henry
old: The "Later" postscript is written as news of the Union defeat at First Bull Run reaches Washington. Henry's regiment is ordered to move — the capital is in panic. The shift from mundane daily life ("I want to get a shirt washed") to "There has been a hard battle today" in a single letter is one of the most dramatic moments in the collection.
final: Writing from Washington, Henry fills most of this letter to his sister Frances with the ordinary rhythm of camp — five hours of daily drill, the Colonel's praise drawing three cheers, two newspapers to pass the dull hours, a dollar begged to wash a shirt. Then a postscript breaks the calm: "We are ordered off... There has been a hard battle today." He doesn't yet know it is Bull Run, only to leave by morning — and tells her not to send the money after all.

author: james
old: First letter from James in the collection. Documents his time at West Point.
final: Filtering letters near Manassas, Henry writes to his mother that the regiment has marched into Virginia and lies in camp three miles from the enemy, with pickets exchanging fire daily. He plays down the danger — he is well, the food is plain but plenty — yet asks her to direct his next letter carefully, as if uncertain where he will be. A son steadies his mother even as the army gathers him in.

author: henry
old: Camp life update with details on guard duty along the Potomac and accidental death in regiment.
final: From the Washington defenses, Henry reports his regiment posted as Potomac guards against rebel crossings — and the camp talk that it may never see a battle, to which he answers, "I for one am willing to go. I don't care where." Three days too sick to drill, sleeping on wet ground in fever-and-ague country, he still sends his five-dollar gold piece home by the Captain, ordering his sister and mother to spend it: "I put that down as a command."

author: henry
old: References Battle of Hatteras Inlet (Aug 28-29, 1861), Henry's advice against Alexander enlisting, cannon fire into Virginia, and rumor of wintering in Kentucky. Important for Alexander's enlistment timeline.
final: From the Washington defenses after coming off picket with Corporal Kellogg, Henry counsels his mother that Alexander "had better stay at home" rather than join "Ransoms Company" — college or home over war. Word has just reached camp of the fall of Fort Hatteras, "a noble achievement," and he wagers the war can't last two years. His regiment's two brass cannon lobbed shells three miles into Virginia last Sabbath, but the enemy "would not return the favor."

author: alexander
old: Alexander's first letter in the collection — documents his arrival at military barracks in Ogdensburgh. Vivid arrival scene with sensory detail.
final: Alexander's first letter home, written from the Ogdensburgh barracks: "Here I am safe and sound... How strange it does seem. Ah! what a bedlam!" He marvels at hemlock-board berths stuffed with straw, the parade ground ringed with armed sentinels, and a half-tipsy soldier on the cars who hollered for the fifer and drummer to "strike up." Dinner was soup, boiled pork, and potatoes — but it was the ginger bread from home that "went well."

author: henry
old: Brief update with interesting detail of Confederate signal flare observed from picket duty.
final: On picket duty near Washington, Henry watches a Confederate signal rise over Virginia — "somewhat like the evening star, only it was a dark red — looked very fine." Between such glimpses of the enemy he relays the small comforts of camp: a merry supper with Lieutenant Scott, word that a friend from Chazy Village addressed his last letter, and a note for Mother that he already has more clothing than he can carry.

author: henry
old: Confirms Alexander has officially enlisted ("in for the war"). False alarm incident at camp. Money being sent home via Reich.
final: Henry takes in the news that his brother Alexander has gone "in for the war," answering it with measured resignation — "Perhaps it is all for the best" — and the quiet conviction it "can't last a great while." From camp near Washington, where bombs are lobbed into Virginia and jittery guards have just fired on a white horse in a false alarm, he wraps twenty-five dollars to send home and prepares to head out two days on picket in the first cold snap of fall.

author: alexander
old: Detailed daily schedule at Camp Wheeler. Company sworn into state service on Saturday (Sept 21). Regiment over 700 men. Election of officers — Capt. Ransom and Lt. Loring E. White.
final: At Camp Wheeler in Ogdensburg, nineteen-year-old Alexander walks his sister through a soldier's full day — reveille at six, drill after breakfast, a twelve-pound brass field piece fired at sunrise and sunset. His company was sworn into state service Saturday after a rigid exam; the surgeon called him "a fine boy." He asks for Henry's overcoat, "tucked up so that it will not be too long for me," a small line that measures the boy inside the uniform.

author: alexander
old: Vivid guard duty narrative — watch word compromised, guards doubled, Colonel's response. Rich detail on camp security procedures. Daily prayer meetings documented.
final: On guard duty as sentry No. 11 at Camp Wheeler, Alexander Hubbell passed five men through his post in the dark before catching a whispered "is it right" — the watch word had leaked. He called out the Officer of the Guard, the watch was doubled, and the Colonel ordered any man who ran the guard shot through the legs. Off duty, he wrote a letter for a fellow who couldn't, and found unexpected comfort in a Methodist prayer meeting, thirty or forty strong.

author: henry
old: Detailed camp life: tent improvements, guard duty, rations, card-playing ban. Corrects exaggerated report of a skirmish.
final: Writing to brother Charles, Henry corrects an inflated report of an attack across the river — not three companies of Rebels but thirty-five men against twelve — quipping, "I wonder you did not hear there was a thousand." He recounts a bad bout of rheumatism from sleeping on bare ground, eased only after he and two tentmates splurged 95 cents on a tent floor, and admits he held off writing of his illness because he couldn't spell the word.

author: alexander
old: Documents the "Brother Craftsmen" mutual aid society — soldier fraternal organization with headquarters at Watertown, NY. Detailed description of camp prayer meeting. Reveals Alexander's moral framework and social isolation.
final: Alexander, barely a week into camp at Camp Wheeler near Ogdensburgh, writes his mother in genuine distress: offered the office of Adjutant in the "Brother Craftsmen," a mutual-aid society that vows to rescue brothers "if sore pressed in battle," he keeps asking "What shall I do?" Sickened by camp vice, he confesses he has "no friends in the Reg." and begs her to consult Mr. Copeland.

author: alexander
old: Brief logistics letter — uniforms arriving, furlough promised, travel pass needed.
final: Nearly broke two weeks into camp, Alexander asks his mother to spare him a three-dollar fare he cannot afford: a railroad pass from Mr. Hoyle so he can come home on furlough the moment his uniform arrives Saturday. Even his postage is rationed — he tucks a letter to Henry inside hers to save the cost, confessing he has barely enough to settle his washing bill until a dollar or two arrives from the State.

author: alexander
old: Camp description, regiment numbers, company strength. Mentions possible corporal's berth for Alexander.
final: Camp Wheeler, a mile and a half from Ogdensburgh, was filling fast: the regiment counted some 800 men marching toward its full thousand, Alexander's company already 60 or 70 strong of a planned 101. Writing his brother, he confessed he liked soldiering "very well so far" — the fare excellent, the captain kind, a corporal's berth and a furlough both within reach. He'd bathed in the Lawrence the day before and enjoyed it famously. "Don't you envy me."

author: henry
old: Entire company under arrest over rope-cutting incident. Lt. Scott conflict. Military punishment details. Charles considering enlistment — Henry says join his company if he does. Chaplain sick.
final: A disciplinary crisis grips Henry's company near Washington: a soldier who left his picket early and grew abusive to Lt. Scott had his pay docked, a 30-lb knapsack strapped on, and his hands tied above his head — until a comrade cut the rope, throwing the whole company under arrest. From picket duty, the eighteen-year-old vows he "tries to do what is right," even as card-playing now brings court martial and his brother Charles grows anxious to enlist.

author: henry
old: Brigadier General Gormon's inspection; regiment called "sharp shooters" in press. POW escape narrative — Kellogg confirmed prisoner in Richmond. Murder by stabbing in camp. Poolesville winter quarters rumor. James confirmed in school.
final: Henry relays a daring escape from rebel captivity: a prisoner taken in the same skirmish as Kellogg feigned illness to hoard his daily ration of opium, then drugged his guard's coffee and slipped through three enemy regiments to reach camp — bringing word that Kellogg is held unwounded at Richmond. Henry also notes a man stabbed by a drunk at midnight, dead by morning, and the 34th lately christened "the sharp shooters" in the papers.

author: henry
old: Receipt of handmade portfolio from Frances. Mentions Brink (family connection). Nellie correspondence.
final: From the camps around Washington, Henry thanks his sister Frances for a handmade portfolio of writing supplies — so finely made he refused to believe it wasn't store-bought ("I thought it came form the store"), now the envy of the other boys, who have theirs but none to match it. Beneath the gratitude runs a quieter homesickness: he longs for her picture and a chance to sing when she has company. A postscript notes a letter from Nellie, with a photograph promised.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's regiment confirmed: 60th NY Infantry ("Sixtieth Regt. Detailed journey narrative: Camp Wheeler → Rouses Point → Whitehall → Albany → Hudson River → New York City (flag & horse presentation, Enfield rifles iss...
final: At Camp Jackson, three miles from Baltimore, Alexander recounts to his mother a nine-day march from Camp Wheeler to the war: dawn past West Point ("the most beautiful I ever saw"), a flag and bay horse presented in New York, a Philadelphia breakfast of beef and sauerkraut, and five rounds of cartridges issued before marching through Baltimore. A hungry stretch the men dubbed "Starvation Heights" tested them. "I think of all of you often, very, very, often," he closes.

author: henry
old: Henry now at Camp McClellan — regiment has moved from Washington defenses. Battle formation false alarm (rebels crossing river).
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in a cold November rain, Henry tells brother Charles his regiment may see a battle before winter — and recounts the night the whole brigade was formed in line of battle and marched toward the river on a false report that the rebels were crossing. Between the soldiering he sends $20 home by express, registers quiet shock at Albert Savage's death, and asks that Mother be told her preserves arrived safely.

author: henry
old: Confederate deserter crossing Potomac at night — vivid eyewitness account. Describes visible enemy (fires along river, visible in daytime). Informal cross-river trading/contact despite orders.
final: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his brother James of a drunken Confederate deserter who paddled a half-swamped boat across the Potomac to surrender to Henry's twelve-man picket post — cursing the sentries as "sons of biches" when they demanded the countersign, then refusing to go back when the rebels called him the next morning. Henry kept two rebel gun caps as souvenirs; Lt. Scott paid five dollars for the deserter's knife.

author: henry
old: Brigade composition confirmed: Gorman is General. Brigade includes three NY regiments (including 2nd NY), Minnesota regiment, and 34th NY.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry sketches his brigade's order of battle: three New York regiments including the 2nd, the Minnesota regiment, and his own 34th NY, all drilling together two or three times a week under General Gorman. He has shaken off a bout of homesickness and gently corrects the rumors reaching home that his company has suffered — "It is not correct" — admitting only one hard stretch in Virginia.

author: henry
old: Winter conditions, furlough queue, Thanksgiving on picket, picture taken, farm concerns, tax willingness.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in cold so sharp he can scarcely hold his pen, Henry begs his worrying mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease," reports he stands third or fourth in the furlough queue, and came off picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock. He confesses he sometimes thinks he "did wrong to leave home" with the farm needing him that winter, yet pledges that "when I do get home I shall stay."

author: alexander
old: Alexander's unit definitively confirmed: Co. H, 60th NY Volunteers ("Sixtieth Regt.
final: Alexander's first army pay reaches Camp Jackson — and he sends fifteen of his seventeen dollars home, half-joking he'll have his Mother "courtmartialed" if she won't buy herself a warm winter cloak. He recounts a sentry's rifle going off on the picket bridge, taking off a man's thumb, and now cautions his own reliefs to carry their arms with care. He clings to the verse Frances wrote in his Bible — "God is our refuge and strength."

author: alexander
old: James had Orderly Sergeant offer (needed 5 men) — turned it down. James has chance at West Point — Alexander strongly encourages education over enlistment.
final: Alexander writes from Camp Jackson, near Baltimore, having finally received four home letters in a bunch — "I feel about five hundred per cent better" — after a lost knapsack swallowed his earlier letter and writing materials. At Charley's request he sketches camp life minute by minute, from the half-past-five reveille to the day's rations of bread, beef, and green coffee. Then he turns urgent: James must never give up the idea of an education — "Never — never, never."

author: alexander
old: Photography details — two pictures taken in Baltimore (one with Luther, one solo). Shows photographic economy of Civil War soldiers.
final: His furious sketch of a Baltimore swindle: Alexander tells Mother two "pictures" cost thirteen shillings, lamenting "that which is dearly bought is apt to be prized." The first portrait so enraged him he "felt like making a bayonet charge upon the one who took it," vowing a better likeness "if it costs me fifty dollars." The joint photograph with Luther he asks her to hide away and show no one — "a memorial of our soldiering together."

author: alexander
old: Eyewitness account of freight train boiler explosion — one of the most detailed civilian/military incident narratives in the collection. Ransom's miraculous survival.
final: Capt. Ransom climbs aboard a passing freight train during the "Grand Rounds" near Camp Jackson — and survives a boiler explosion that kills everyone else on the engine. Alexander gives his sister Frances a harrowing, almost forensic account: the engineer hurled hundreds of feet through a tree, the iron dome flung thirty rods, the fireman left burning in a ditch until Ransom puts out the flames with his bare hands. Not even a scratch on him.

author: henry
old: Winter quarters forming — Minnesota regiments building log houses, 34th NY building hospital. Tent mates identified (E. Graves from Chazy, John Green, A. Perkins). Sutler drummed out for selling liquor. Colonel L--- resigned (considered coward). Henry hasn't connected with Alexander yet — wrong address.
final: From Camp McClellan, two days before Christmas, Henry expects the 34th New York to settle into winter quarters guarding the Potomac — the Minnesota regiments are raising log houses and his own regiment is building a hospital, signs enough that "this looks somewhat like staying." He watches discipline tighten: the old sutler drummed out for selling liquor, gamblers made to stand on a barrel six hours without food. Still unable to reach his brother Alexander, he confesses he gets very lonesome now and then.

author: henry
old: B. Miner carrying letters to Champlain (private mail carrier). Accordion lessons from Bill Robers. Journal discontinued due to cold — Henry regrets this. Eight rebel deserters crossed to Union side, report rebels have nothing to eat. Capt. Rich preached. Poolesville ~3 miles from camp.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry reports eight rebels crossing the lines as deserters with word that the enemy "have nothing to eat" — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac. With little else to tell in the sameness of winter quarters, he confesses the cold has stopped his journal, a thing he'll be sorry for if he gets home, and admits he'd give much to be back for the village sing school.

author: henry
old: Brigade drill — Gen. Gorman complimented 34th NY ("did the best of them all"). Henry still can't reach Alexander — directed to Washington but that's wrong (should be Baltimore). Henry doesn't know Alexander's regiment. Moral commentary on swearing and gambling. Same gambling punishment as LTR-1861-12-19-001. Accidental self-shooting in Minnesota Regt.
final: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry writes home with a soldier's pride: at brigade drill, Gen. Gorman told the regiment "they did the best of them all" — "we felt quite proud, I tell you." Yet he still cannot reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington on a direction now proving wrong: "It seems bad that we cannot correspond." Unsettled by the swearing and gambling around him, Henry insists a man keeps good morals in camp only if "very strict and firm."

author: alexander
old: Company H moved to Baltimore proper — ordered to replace Company C at Camden Station (B&O Railroad depot). Quartered in 3-story brick building on city outskirts.
final: Company H, singled out as one of the best in the regiment, is pulled by Colonel Hayward into Baltimore to replace Company C guarding Camden Station, the Baltimore & Ohio depot. Alexander writes from a three-story brick building where five tentmates sing and brew tea on the Captain's stove. Promoted from seventh to fourth Corporal in three months, he still grumbles, playfully: a soldier who writes twice to their once, and feels neglected.

author: alexander
old: Preston King in Baltimore — U. Senator from NY, reportedly trying to have 60th NY sent north to guard frontiers (Trent Affair context).
final: Preston King is in Baltimore, Alexander reports, "trying to have the Regiment sent North to guard the frontiers" — and so, the corporal hints, he may be home sooner than expected. Yet his Christmas turns wistful: "I a soldier hundreds of miles from home! How funny, eh?" He delights that the white cow has a new "bossy," marches seven men out to relieve the pickets, and adds that Mason and "Stidell" have reportedly been released.

author: henry
old: Henry finally received a letter from Alexander — direction "not quite correct" but it arrived. Alexander wrote about Capt.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from his brother Alexander — the letter found him despite a direction "not quite correct" — and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between buying a $3.50 sheet-iron stove against the cold and a promise to send $25 home next pay day, Henry sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.

author: alexander
old: Most detailed guard duty description in entire collection — sentinel orders verbatim, corporal relief procedures, 2-hour rotation, night firing protocol, camp alarm sequence.
final: At Camp Jackson the sentinel's challenge ran word for word — "Number ### — Advance" — and after three unheeded halts at night, each guard fired his piece to alarm the camp. Writing from Baltimore, Alexander sets down a corporal's day with an ethnographer's care: two-hour relief rotations, a king's-worthy kettle of beef, pared potatoes and cabbage, his own long vigils by the fire. On New Year's morning he pictures James reading the January Harper's at home.

author: alexander
old: NCO warrant received — formal appointment as Corporal, with commission language quoted verbatim ("Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence in the patriotism, valor, fidelity and abilities of Alexander F.
final: Alexander writes from Baltimore on New Year's Day, 1862, exhausted from a night's guard duty as the city's revelers "made quite a racket" — but proud to report his warrant as a non-commissioned officer, a corporal's equivalent of an officer's commission. He quotes its grand opening verbatim: "Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence... in Alexander F. Hubbell." Tired and "really ashamed" of the brief note, he still thanks the family for the welcome postage stamps.

author: henry
old: New Year's 1862 at Camp McClellan: Beer from Captain, some boys drunk. Company presented Capt.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan after a New Year's of beer "from the Capt." and a few boys gone too drunk, Henry tells his mother his company has presented Capt. Reich a $125 sword — he gave a dollar on a private's pay, "some gave more and some less." The Minnesota band played most all night before the Colonel's tent. He longs for a furlough, but only married men may go, so he waits — lonesome for letters and the box of socks still stuck in Washington.

author: henry
old: Henry burned all home letters — knapsack space and anticipation of moving into Virginia. "Please burn all my letters" — if obeyed, this would have destroyed the home-side correspondence.
final: From Camp McClellan, Henry adds a few lines to his sister Frances and admits he has burned every letter he received from home: they took up too much room in his knapsack, and he did not want them on him "if I should go over into Virginia." Then his postscript turns the request around — "Please burn all my letters." He closes glad, for her sake, that she is going to teach in Montreal this winter — a quiet aside beside a plea that, obeyed, would have erased this entire correspondence.

author: alexander
old: H killed January 9 — Alexander helped recover the body ("screwed up" courage). Quotes Henry's letter (mailed Jan 6): "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living" — a prescient statement...
final: Alexander writes home from Baltimore, frantic that no letter has come since December 20 — "Are you all sick or are you dead?" Then the harder news: a picket from his own Company was killed on the ninth, and he helped bring in the body, "a sight that but few of our Company could bear." He quotes Henry's New Year letter — "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living" — glad his brother "had not forgotten his God."

author: alexander
old: Moved to first platoon / headquarters — replacing Corporal Myers (sick). Now "at head quarters.
final: Lonely at Camden Station, Baltimore, Alexander hasn't heard from home since December 22 and conjures Champlain swept off by the Chazy River or buried in snow until "the Sixtieth" digs them out. Ordered to replace the ailing Corporal Myers, he writes now from "head quarters" in the first platoon, wonders whether to buy a revolver for hauling off armed drunken soldiers, and signs himself "Corporal A. F. Hubbell" — a precious Bible his one comfort.

author: alexander
old: Porter (Edwin Porter) killed by train on railroad track — graphic eyewitness account. Alexander helped recover body.
final: Porter has been killed upon the track. Roused from a mattress at a sick mess-mate's side, Alexander joined the squad that found him three-quarters of a mile out, "literally cut in two." Writing from Camden Station, Baltimore, he records the inquest and the funeral with a soldier's exactness — corporal and eight men, arms reversed, three volleys over the vault — then turns, stung, to defend why he enlisted: not "for the novelty," but to fight for his native land.

author: alexander
old: Union Relief Association described — private/government funded, feeds soldiers passing through Baltimore; seating for 800+, sleeping room for a regiment. Alexander boarded there at Camden Station.
final: At Camden Station's Union Relief Association — sustained by private gift and government, with seats for eight hundred men and sleeping room for a regiment — Alexander Hubbell found meals that "saved the soldiers from a great deal of suffering," and writes "God bless the Association," for he had boarded there himself. Hearing brother James may win an appointment, his joy breaks loose: "Hurrah! Hurrah!" He sends home twenty dollars to fit James off.

author: henry
old: Pay day accounting: $15 sent home; sutler bill $5. 50); owes band 50¢, cook 50¢, sword $1.
final: Paid off at Camp McClellan, Henry sends $15 home and itemizes a soldier's whole economy from $13-a-month pay — sutler, boots, a $1 sword installment, fifty cents each to the band and the cook. He turns down requests to lend money in camp: "I would rather send it home." Buoyed by the "glorious victory in Kentucky," he predicts the war will end before July, even as the unhealthy barracks are burned for firewood, leaving the men in tents for the rest of winter.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's near-miss with train — passenger train "hardly ten feet from me," one desperate jump to safety. Edwin Porter confirmed killed by cars (same incident as LTR-1862-01-17-001).
final: Alexander, guarding the rails at Baltimore, looks back to see a passenger train "hardly ten feet from me" — "I gave one jump. Jump — that don't half express it." Days earlier the same cars had killed a comrade, Edwin Porter. Writing his sister in Canada, he charges her to defend the Union with her tongue if not arms: "I charge you be valiant." A near-miss told with grin and grief in the same breath.

author: alexander
old: Colonel Hayward resigned — 60th NY now "Orphan Regiment. " New Colonel Green expected.
final: Colonel Hayward's resignation has left the 60th NY styled the "Orphan Regiment," though Alexander tells his brother Charles they may be better off without a colonel, hoping new Colonel Green proves "smart and brave." Writing a little each day from Baltimore, he reports measles thinning the ranks — one man so low at the hospital he "was rolled over twice to ascertain whether he was dead or alive" — but none lost from his own well-tended Company.

author: henry
old: Two desertions from Co. D — one from drunken scrape/guard house, one while cutting wood (when Captain was in Champlain).
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in a thaw he hopes has "broke" the heart of winter, Henry tallies two desertions from his company: one man drank himself into the guard house and bolted, another vanished to cut wood while the Captain was home in Champlain. Amid gambling and watch lotteries he won't touch, the young soldier guards his pay and his pledge not to drink, and sits twice for photographs beside his tent-mate Graves.

author: henry
old: 34th NY and Gorman's Brigade marched to Harpers Ferry. Departed Camp McClellan → 20-mile march → camped overnight (cold, no shelter) → Adams Town → 30-mile freight train ride → Harpers Ferry.
final: Writing from Camp Gorman, two miles from Harpers Ferry, Henry recounts his regiment's hard march to the front: twenty miles the first day, a freezing night under only blankets and sky, up at three for coffee and a hard cracker. A freight train carried them to a town he finds "a perfect wreck" — buildings burnt to their walls, the bridge gone, a locomotive in the river, all the rebels' work. Crossing the Potomac on a bridge of boats, the 34th was called the best-looking regiment to pass over.

author: henry
old: Detailed march narrative — parallel account to LTR-1862-02-05-001 with additional details: passed through Barnesville; "very short notice" to march; Col.
final: Writing to his brother Charles from Camp Bolivar Heights, Henry recounts the 34th's sudden march on "very short notice" — out at three a.m. on coffee, hard crackers, and salt junk, through Barnesville to Adamstown, then thirty miles by freight car into Harpers Ferry behind Col. Ladue. Billeted in a cotton factory, the men ground its stored wheat through the floors until Gen. Gorman laughed he "did not know what to do with them." Crammed seventeen to a bell tent, Henry would rather be home to make sugar this spring, "but that is out of the question."

author: henry
old: Routine morale letter from winter quarters. Documents camp conditions, religious provisions (Testament and Psalms), and clarifies a false rumor about Lt. Scott's loyalty. Provides timeline checkpoint: Henry enlisted ~June 1, sworn in June 15, in service ~9 months by this date.
final: Writing from a bell tent at Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, his letter steadied on his knee for want of a table, Henry sets his mother's mind at rest about a rumor that had traveled all the way home: Lieut. Scott was arrested not for communicating with the rebels but for falling asleep as officer of the guard. Some in the company dislike Scott; Henry says he likes him very well himself. He prizes the company's gift of a Testament and Psalms.

author: alexander
old: Shows inter-regimental communication: Alexander (60th NY, Baltimore) exchanges letters with Henry (34th NY, likely at different location), indicates family network among brothers in service. Demonstrates officer kindness (Capt. Ransom) and shows regiments receiving civilian visitors/correspondence from Poolesville area. Alludes to James's academic situation and family pressure to succeed (pre-West Point confirmation).
final: Capt. Ransom paid out of his own pocket for the company's fifteen-cent photographs rather than let his men cover it — a small act of officer kindness Alexander, writing his mother from Baltimore on Feb. 7, 1862, thought worth reporting home. He swaps news of letters to Charles, Henry, and Frances, laughs off a Poolesville "Valentine" mocking him as a "raw recruit," and turns anxious over James: "It will not be him alone that will suffer if he fails."

author: alexander
old: CRITICAL SOURCE: West Point appointment for James Hubbell CONFIRMED as of Feb. This is a major turning point in the Hubbell family narrative.
final: Alexander's reply lands with brotherly thunder: word has reached Baltimore that James has won an appointment to West Point. "How proud I shall feel of you," he writes, "Why, man, I shan't see my boots for a week" — urging James to study hard and "put your best foot forward," since the academy would spare him years of toil. Between fresh-issued blue pants and dish-washing, Alexander promises he'll come home "quite a cook."

author: henry
old: CRITICAL CHRONOLOGICAL ANCHOR: Henry's presence at Camp McClellan on Feb. 11 — 13, 1862, directly contradicts the Feb.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry answers Charles's question about soldiers allotting pay home with an unvarnished ledger of camp life: many in his company blow their wages at the sutler's, including George Dodds, now borrowing — though Henry asks Charles not to repeat it. He details the ration cycle and the indignity of eating "dog fashion" without tin plates, joking that "a pound or two of dirt" is "good enough for soldiers."

author: henry
old: Eyewitness reporting of major Civil War victory: Henry documents the Burnside Expedition's victory in South Carolina (Battle of Roanoke Island, Feb.
final: Writing to his sister Frances from Camp McClellan, Henry passes the night's electric news: word of "the glorious victory in South Carolina" by the Burnside Expedition, two thousand prisoners taken, met with "great cheering" through the camp. Eager and untested, he boasts that once the 34th New York goes into action "the rebels will have to run" — then notes, plainly, that the farms in this country are "all worked by slaves."

author: henry
old: Brief morale letter from Camp McClellan. Provides snapshot of soldier experience: guard duty as most difficult aspect, drunkenness and fighting in company, mild weather, homesickness. Reports receiving multiple letters from Alexander (evidence of inter-regimental correspondence). Shows mother's letters as significant morale booster.
final: Writing from Camp McClellan in mud and unseasonably mild weather, Henry calls guard duty "the hardest of soldiering" — up nearly all night — yet admits he has grown so used to it he hardly minds, and longs to "make a move of some kind." He grieves the heavy drunkenness and fighting in his company but insists he keeps clear of it all, and tells his mother that nothing does a soldier so much good as a letter from home.

author: alexander
old: MULTI-FACETED MAJOR SOURCE: (1) Alexander's college decision: He declines college at this moment, preferring to stay in service and work farm/family business. Plans to be "well fitted" before attending.
final: Corporal A. F. Hubbell, not quite eighteen, writes home from Baltimore with a chilling tale: a Union picket took a "home made cake" from a woman in a covered carriage and was poisoned near to death, frothing and vomiting green before castor oil and turpentine saved him. Alexander declines his mother's offer of college — better the open air than to "shut myself up" — and reports new dark-blue corporal's stripes as his brigade hopes for South Carolina.

author: alexander
old: Documents soldier's sabbath observance, religious life, and church attendance in occupied Baltimore. Shows postal economics of war period and family postage hardship. Provides evidence of inter-company communication (Corporal Perkins, Henry's messmate). Reveals family correspondence delays and Aunt Laurie's negligent letter-writing. Establishes Alexander's playful tone and humor. Request for Plattsburgh (NY) newspaper indicates interest in home region news.
final: At seventeen, on "the holy sabbath" in occupied Baltimore, Alexander writes Mother from the quiet of the quarters, having just heard "a very good discourse on death" at the Sharp St. M.E. church. He cannot answer Henry's letter or Corporal Perkins's for want of a single postage stamp — and gently proposes setting aside part of his next pay so Mother can buy stamps too, recalling she once went silent for lack of them. He teases that Aunt Laurie has "turned rebel."

author: henry
old: Orders to march — knapsacks packed, ready at a moment's notice. Read at dress parade.
final: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother the order has come: read at dress parade, the men are to pack knapsacks and stand ready to march at a moment's notice, surplus clothes boxed off to Poolesville. The night before, the chaplain preached on "the Duty of Patriotism" and doubted they'd see another Sabbath in camp — heavy firing already sounding across the river. Henry closes, as always, urging his mother not to worry: he has good health now.

author: henry
old: RESOLVES DATING DISCREPANCY: "Our Regt. Left Camp McClellan on the 26th.
final: Henry writes from Harpers Ferry that the regiment "Left Camp McClellan on the 26th," marching through Poolesville, Barnesville, and Adamstown, then taking the cars to a pontoon bridge of boats into the gutted town. He counts perhaps 60,000 troops massed here and, eager for what's coming, confesses he doesn't care how soon they "see some fun." Yet the burnt bridge, brick walls standing over ashes, and wrecked arsenal leave him feeling "bad" at the rebels' destruction.

author: henry
old: Short addendum. Confirms Henry's regiment is in a grist mill building (previously described as cotton factory in LTR-1862-02-05-002). Rebels took wheat from this location. Too restricted to explore town (guards posted).
final: Henry writes from a large brick building that once served as a grist mill — a place, he notes wryly, where the rebels seized so much wheat "they will never have the same chance again." On a cold but pleasant March day, kept from roaming the town and from mailing his letter, he apologizes for falling short of the longer letter he'd hoped to send and promises more when he can.

author: alexander
old: Duck hunting adventure — vivid narrative of soldiers hunting in Chesapeake Bay with rifles; fog, leaking boat, broken oarlock.
final: Corporal A. F. Hubbell writes his sister Frances a tale of soldiers gone duck hunting with rifles in Baltimore — so much fog they couldn't find their kills, in a leaking boat with a broken oarlock. The next day Lt. Fitch and Corporal Luther nearly "got ducked" themselves when a gale swamped their boat; they leapt to a pier and lost the boat, Luther's share five dollars. He waves off a wild rumor that Gen. Banks's division — Henry's — was cut to pieces.

author: alexander
old: James's War Department appointment confirmed — studying under Everest. Alexander wishes he could send $60.
final: James's appointment from the War Department has come through, and Alexander, newly mustered in at Baltimore and watching cavalry drill swords "till their wrists fairly ache," only wishes he could raise the $60 to send his brother. He delights in news of the hens, the heifer, and eight pounds of butter a week. A postscript reports the 34th at Harpers Ferry as "the van of the advancing army," and a Co. C picket struck by a train, his leg broken and head terribly wounded.

author: alexander
old: Massive troop movements through Baltimore: 3-4,000 on Sunday alone; thousands more coming. 30 steamers for Fortress Monroe.
final: Massive troop movements funnel through Baltimore: three or four thousand soldiers on Sunday alone, with thirty steamers and sixty boats waiting to ferry New York regiments to Fortress Monroe. On guard duty, Corporal Alexander confides darker scenes — drawing his sabre on a drunken runaway, a man seizing him by the hair — then begs his mother to tell no one: the boys hold it a point of honor.

author: henry
old: March to Winchester and back — 34th NY and two brigades marched 30 miles from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester, found 25,000 Union troops already there. Rebels had left "probably for good.
final: Henry's regiment and two brigades marched some thirty miles on foot from Harpers Ferry toward Winchester to drive out the rebels, only to learn three miles short of the town that 25,000 Union troops already held it and the Confederates had fled "probably for good." Henry pulled picket and skirmish duty after twenty miles and owns to "a good many hardships" — yet nine months from home, he still hopes the rebellion will be over by next summer.

author: alexander
old: Refuses to burn letters — "No — no — I cannot do that. " Has kept all letters since enlistment (except some from Ogdensburg).
final: Alexander, writing his mother from Baltimore on March 17, 1862, refuses her plea to burn his letters — "No — no — I cannot do that" — having kept nearly every one since enlisting. He describes guard duty in a fierce storm, a rubber blanket sluicing water until a gallon pooled in each pant leg, and confesses he was "gulled" out of five dollars by an Excelsior Brigade sergeant who vanished. Of his country he loves it now "ten times ten times."

author: henry
old: Bell tents detailed: 16 men, bell-shaped stove in center, pole in middle, open top for smoke. Roads to Winchester: macadamized (small stone), very good in any weather.
final: Writing from Camp Gorman on Bolivar Heights, Henry tells his brother James the brigade expects to move soon for Washington, and that the Shenandoah railroad bridge is repaired so the cars again run to Winchester over good macadamized roads. Sixteen men share his bell-shaped tent, a bell stove at its center and the top open for smoke. He confesses a long-neglected debt for Mrs. Douglas's flour, asks James to settle it from his money, and adds wearily that he wouldn't object if the war closed next week.

author: henry
old: 34th NY moves from Harpers Ferry to Washington — 83 miles by freight train in 24 hours. Arrived ~2 AM, marched 1+ mile to brick barracks.
final: After the railroad bridge at Harpers Ferry was finished, Henry's 34th New York rode a freight train eighty-three miles to Washington in twenty-four hours, reaching brick barracks at two in the morning to await pay before an unknown assignment. A Sabbath in the capital, he marvels, feels nothing like one — cars running, soldiers drunk, the provost guard hauling stragglers to the guardhouse — and he vows to keep his pass signed and dodge arrest himself.

author: alexander
old: 60th NY "struck tents" — moved from Eutaw St. quarters to Camp Preston King near Baltimore.
final: Alexander writes from Camp Preston King near Baltimore — a hasty "dispatch," not a letter. The 60th has "struck tents" again, left its Eutaw St. quarters, and may move for Fortress Monroe within ten days. He sketches his Colonel in one stroke: a "savage looking old fellow" with a beard of "wolfish gray," who threatens to resign if the regiment isn't pulled off road duty. Only James stays silent, and Alex vows to pull his ears when he gets home.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's 18th birthday — March 28, 1862 (writing March 30, reflecting on it). I have begun life's battle for myself.
final: Alexander spent his eighteenth birthday on a nine-mile march, then wrote home from Relay House on a sheet he labeled "Dispatch No. 2." His regiment had just struck tents again, brigaded as the "Railroad Brigade" and rumored bound for Harpers Ferry to guard the line. "I feel old," he tells his mother. "I have begun life's battle for myself. I am thrown upon my own resources." Surrounded by sin and vice, he writes, he feels strong in the Lord.

author: alexander
old: COMPLETE DAILY SCHEDULE: 6 AM roll call → 7 breakfast → 8 guard mounting → 9 NCO drill → 10 squad drill → 11:30 inspection → 12:30 dinner → 2:30 company drill → 4:30 dress parade → 6 supper → 9 PM roll call → 9:30 taps.
final: Beauregard is massing rebels at Corinth, and Alexander watches from Relay House for word of whether Grant or his rival will prove "the greatest general." His day runs from six AM roll call to nine-thirty taps, every hour drilled and inspected. But the heat is personal: a 200-acre swindle near Riders gnaws at him, and of his Confederate kin he writes he could "draw sight with my rifle on Octove or Julio with a very steady hand." Then marching orders arrive — "Joy, joy, joy."

author: henry
old: 34th NY moves to the Peninsula — Alexandria → steamboat → Fortress Monroe → Hampton, VA. ~200 miles in 2 days.
final: Henry writes from Hampton, Va., after the 34th New York's two-day steamboat passage from Alexandria to Fortress Monroe — nearly 200 miles down a Chesapeake so wide he saw no land on either side. He finds the town burned to the ground, "worse than Harpers Ferry, every building burnt," the men penned like sheep, sleeping four rubber blankets buttoned into a tent. Hard crackers, no coffee — "but then we are soldiers," he shrugs, "and have to put up with whatever comes."

author: henry
old: Henry keeping a journal — "I have been keeping a Journal some time. " Plans to copy and send home.
final: Writing by candlelight near Fortress Monroe with roll call minutes away, Henry tells his mother he has been "keeping a Journal some time" he means to copy and send home — even as his regiment marches twenty-four miles to York Town at dawn, expecting an onward movement toward Richmond. The rebels have made "a clean sweep of everything," and a peddler who wandered into camp was stripped of his pies and apples in moments. Yet it is the tree toads that make him think of home.

author: henry
old: 25,000 troops at Hampton with one brigade. Steamer ran aground — had to transfer.
final: Writing his brother Charles from a green Hampton, Va. field shared by some twenty-five thousand troops, Henry recounts a crowded two-and-a-half-day boat passage whose steamer ran aground, forcing a transfer to reach shore. Confident after a summer of bayonet drill — "I pity the rebels" — he still confesses he would rather be making sugar this spring than soldiering, and urges Charles not to let out the home sugar bush except to an honest man.

author: henry
old: Pocket diary confirmed — "I have been keeping a pocket diary, write down everything that transpires from day to day. I have 28 dates.
final: Writing from "Camp in field" as heavy musketry sounds off toward Yorktown, Henry tells his brother James he has been keeping a pocket diary — 28 dated entries recording "everything that transpires from day to day." Two days earlier his company double-quicked a mile expecting a fight; a captured rebel in gray overcoat looked on "very sullen." He urges James toward West Point, yet still asks him to mind the cows and horse, hoping to be home next summer.

author: henry
old: Pioneer duty at Yorktown — detailed as pioneers with axes, picks, shovels; building roads through woods for artillery. Rebels blocked roads.
final: From a nameless "Camp in field" sixteen miles from Hampton, Henry tells his mother how his regiment spent the Sabbath detailed as pioneers — axes, picks, and shovels cutting fresh roads for the artillery through woods the retreating rebels had felled ahead of Yorktown. He records Gen. Gorman's cold counsel to keep cool in action "and not to mind if brother or cousin fell, but to go ahead," then, glimpsing McClellan twice and Virginia trees in blossom, confesses the whole campaign "is all like a dream."

author: henry
old: Rebels at York Town "pretty well surrounded. " Rebel slave reported they left on double quick.
final: Writing from camp sixteen miles from Fortress Monroe after his regiment took the boat from Alexandria, Henry reports the rebels holding York Town but "getting pretty well surrounded," and expects to march there any day for "a little skirmish." He passes along an enslaved man's account that the rebels fled "on a double quick" at word of the Union advance, dismisses them as "a cowardly set," then closes hoping to be home next June, "if the war is over."

author: alexander
old: "The little Corporal" — Alexander's nickname (smallest Corporal in company, positioned on extreme left). DeRochambeau/Yorktown comparison — second siege of Yorktown in American history.
final: At Camp Niles by the Relay House, eighteen-year-old Corporal Alexander frets that the war's "late great victories" may end before he can prove how well he can shoot and use his sabre bayonet: "I should feel rather cheap to come home without having been in one battle at least." He dutifully sends ten dollars home, vowing of his brother's education, "cost money what it may I shall have one."

author: henry
old: Siege of Yorktown firsthand — 3 miles from rebel lines. Called into line for expected skirmish.
final: Writing his brother Charles from camp three miles outside Yorktown, Henry relays his first secondhand battle reports — a repulsed rebel assault on a Union battery and a Vermont regiment so badly hit one company was left with "only twenty." Carried across eight days, the letter closes with a rebel dawn attack and a sharpshooter shot down. "Nothing livens me up more than to hear the firing cannon," Henry confesses — a green soldier still hungry for the fight he hasn't yet faced.

author: henry
old: Siege of Yorktown operations: Drums silenced and band doesn't play — fear of rebel shelling. attacked on picket — night before last, heavy musketry; rebels tried to drive pickets in but failed.
final: From the Yorktown siege lines on April 21st, 1862, Henry writes his brother James that the regiment's drums and band have gone silent "for fear that the rebels will find us out and throw shells into our camp," and recounts a driving-rain midnight alarm when the New York 2nd's pickets, attacked in force, refused to be driven in. Between arms inspections and drills, he confesses he often thinks with pleasure of the spring he and James made maple sugar at home.

author: henry
old: Sedgwick's Division, Gorman Brigade — unit identification confirmed. McClellan described: "Splendid looking fellow, smiling countenance, rides a fine horse," ~200 cavalry bodyguard.
final: Writing from the siege lines near Yorktown, Henry pins down his place in the army — Sedgwick's Division, Gorman's Brigade — and watches a balloon rise each day to spy on the rebel works while McClellan rides past. But the war he describes is quieter: three hours on picket in a dark, rainy night, hearing rebels "pounding and sawing" at their works just beyond sight. Even there, his mind drifts home to the horses, the cattle, and a farm with no one to see to it.

author: alexander
old: promoted to Brig. — General Green, "desendent of old revolutionary hero General Green.
final: Promoted: their colonel, "a desendent of old revolutionary hero General Green," has been made Brigadier General of Volunteers — and word reaches camp that New Orleans has fallen, "the heaviest blow that has been struck at the rebels since the war commenced." But the letter's heart is Alexander's wounded reply to his mother: "I am astonished and ashamed that you have so poor an opinion of me. I should not be ashamed to die in such a cause."

author: henry
old: Pay and financial accounting: 2 months' pay; $20 home; boots $1 (Peter Guyan); sutler $1; cook 50¢; $3. Emerson Smith used all wages.
final: Newly paid for two months at Fortress Monroe's Camp "Windfield Scott," Henry mails $20 home by express and accounts for every cent that remains — a dollar to tap his boots, fifty cents to the cook, three-fifty to spend as he pleases. Opposite a rebel fort our men raise a tower under daily shelling, and Henry rises before daylight braced for an attack he senses is coming. The Sabbath, he notes, goes unkept like any other day.

author: henry
old: $20 enclosed by express. Heavy cannonading at 4 AM. Rebel fort visible from camp. On picket.
final: Writing from camp near York Town on May 1st, Henry encloses twenty dollars by express and tells his mother of a rebel fort plainly visible from his lines and heavy cannonading at four that morning. He scrawled the note between turns at picket, signing only "H.H." and closing with a son's plea to "write often."

author: henry
old: Yorktown evacuated by rebels — Henry inside fortifications. "Immense and very strong.
final: Inside the abandoned Confederate fortifications at Yorktown — "immense and very strong," sandbags head-high — Henry writes from a captured rebel tent, marveling at the strongest works he has ever seen. He recounts his hardest night of soldiering: an all-night march through driving rain and deep mud, halting every ten paces behind stacked divisions, back to camp by two in the morning. The retreating enemy buried shells underfoot, and some of his men have already been hurt by them.

author: henry
old: West Point, VA — on York River, NOT the academy. 20-30 miles from Yorktown, ~30 from Richmond.
final: Writing his sister Frances for the first time in nearly a year, Henry reports his regiment's crowded boat passage from newly evacuated Yorktown to West Point, Virginia — a landing on the York River, he is careful to note, not the Military Academy — about thirty miles from Richmond. He marvels at the rebels' vast abandoned earthworks and dates the Yorktown bombardment to Wednesday, April 16, then promises once more to send the journal he has kept of the campaign.

author: henry
old: Cornwallis surrender spot — "pointed out to me. It was a great sight.
final: From West Point on the York River, twenty-five to thirty miles from Richmond, Henry is shown the spot where Cornwallis surrendered — "a great sight," the Revolution's ground now ringed again by American troops. Word reaches him of the 16th Regiment's skirmish, one company losing sixteen. Then his thoughts turn back to the farm, his mother's summer, and a newspaper stolen before he could finish it.

author: alexander
old: Railroad given up to company by 15th-20th — regiment no longer needed. wagers $25 to $1 discharged within a month.
final: At Camp Niles by the Relay House, Alexander tells his anxious mother the railroad will revert to the Company by mid-month and the regiment will soon be discharged — a lieutenant wagering $25 to $1 on it within a month. He reassures her ("We are all in Gods hands") and recounts the band of the Sixtieth answering a heckling Baltimore secessionist with a furious blast of Yankee Doodle, stones gathered to throw if he showed his head again.

author: henry
old: Camp Alton, West Point, VA — 34th Regt. Near unnamed river emptying into York River (likely Pamunkey or Mattaponi).
final: Writing from Camp Alton near West Point, Va., Henry reckons some hundred thousand troops are massed around him and expects the 34th to move on Richmond any day, trusting that "McClellan is working slow but sure." Word reaches him that Alexander's 60th Regt. may be bound for the same place, and he aches to see his brother. Between the lines he is just a farm boy, asking who is working the garden and where the cows are pastured.

author: alexander
old: Alexander crosses into Virginia — "for the first time planted our feet on the sacred soil of Virginia. " Harpers Ferry — 60th NY now deployed there.
final: Alexander crosses the river and "for the first time planted our feet on the sacred soil of Virginia," writing in haste on his knapsack on the ground at Harpers Ferry. The rebels are not far distant, spies already captured, and a battle is expected — yet he reports himself in excellent health and spirits. In the same breath he tells Mother he has sent James twenty dollars, a brother's promise kept even on the edge of a fight.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's first combat experience. Slept on arms every night since arrival.
final: Alexander writes his mother from Harpers Ferry having slept on his arms every night since arrival, the regiment called out nearly nightly behind a powerful battery: "It does me good to hear our shells shriek and howl over our heads." As Union guns prepare to shell the town and clear out rebel sharpshooters, the few remaining inhabitants are warned to leave. His verdict on it all, in three words: "Such is war." He signs, for the first time, Corporal Hubbell.

author: henry
old: George Dodds in hospital, "run down so you would not know him" — applying for discharge. Henry stood march despite being sick.
final: Marching while sick himself, Henry gently turns aside his mother's offer to come nurse him at the front — "you would be obliged to be on your feet most of the time, and I am afraid it would bring you down sick." His comrade George Dodds is so wasted "you would not know him," now hospitalized and seeking a discharge, while Henry resolves to "stand it through." He encloses ten dollars and asks who is keeping his money.

author: alexander
old: 60th NY marches ~40 miles from Harpers Ferry to Winchester. (Free Footed Virginians)" — mocking Confederate retreat.
final: At Winchester, Alexander writes his mother that he still has "not yet had to shoot at the Rebels," who "took 'leg bail'" and fled — earning, he jokes, the title F.F.V., "Free Footed Virginians." He recounts the forty-mile pursuit from Harpers Ferry: knee-deep mud, sleeping in fence corners near Charlestown "where John Brown was hung," eighteen miles in six hours under full kit. Then the surprise that lights him up — running into Albert H. Cook, "the last person I expected to see here."

author: henry
old: Battle of Fair Oaks aftermath — regiment lost 123 wounded and killed (papers said 150). D lost 2 killed and 10 wounded.
final: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond after the Battle of Fair Oaks, Henry counts himself thankful to have come through unhurt — the regiment lost 123 killed and wounded, his own Company D two killed and ten wounded. Three days sick on quinine, rebel shells whizzing into camp "a caution," he longs for one good meal at home: "even if it wasn't anything but potatoes and salt."

author: henry
old: BATTLE OF FAIR OAKS — FIRSTHAND COMBAT ACCOUNT. "You can have no conception of how exciting it is to be in a battle.
final: Writing from camp five miles from Richmond, Henry gives his brother Charles a firsthand account of the battle of Fair Oaks — the ground shaking, the firing "like a number of men felling trees, only much faster," loading while advancing through woods, and his own forty rounds fired before he ever knew anyone had fallen. A captured secesh tells of Richmond ladies who rode out in carriages to watch Yankees taken, then bore home their own wounded instead. Sick with dysentery, Henry admits he gets lonesome now and then.

author: henry
old: One year of service — "A long year it has been to me. Twelve more months.
final: Writing from camp within five miles of Richmond on the first anniversary of his regiment's muster, Henry reckons that fewer than five hundred men are now fit for duty — "a long year it has been to me." Still weak from a week under the doctor's care, he relays a captured rebel's grudging awe at how fast the Yankees could load and fire, and savors how the carriages of ladies who came to watch the Union defeat were instead pressed into carrying off the Confederate wounded.

author: alexander
old: Detailed foraging account — cherries, chickens, milk, sheep, pig. "Are you not horrified to think you have a hen roost robbing son?
final: Foraging three miles from camp, Alexander climbs cherry trees "bending under their weight," bags a half-dozen fowls, fills his canteen with milk, and dresses chickens by a Virginia pasture — Union rules let him take anything a mile out unless the owner proves his loyalty in writing. "Are you not horrified to think you have a hen roost robbing son?" he teases Mother, arguing those who "precipitated war" deserve the loss.

author: henry
old: Henry's health in serious decline — dysentery "very bad," unable to do duty for over a week, Dr. every morning, quinine and pills.
final: Writing from camp five miles outside Richmond on a Sabbath afternoon, Henry confesses to his mother that he has had the dysentery "very bad," unable to do duty for over a week, reporting to the doctor each morning for quinine and pills as sickness spreads through the regiment. Yet he clings to McClellan's siege "starfing them out," even as he admits he is "about disgusted with soldiering" and dreams of home, where he means to sit down and eat nothing but potatoes.

author: henry
old: FAIR OAKS — BAYONET CHARGE DETAIL: "pushed right in head first. " Came to bayonet charge at woods edge.
final: Writing from camp near Richmond to his brother Charles, Henry recounts a recent bayonet charge in which his regiment "pushed right in head first," halting at the woods' edge to fire low into kneeling rebels before they could volley — by his Colonel's account leaving three hundred dead and wounded. To Charles alone he confesses he is "almost tempted to desert sometimes," held back only by the disgrace and by his mother being all alone.

author: alexander
old: FALSE REPORT of Richmond's capture — "capture of Richmond has just been reported. " Dispatch to Sigel and Slow: Richmond captured after 3 days fighting, 30,000 men "left on the field.
final: On July 1, 1862, Corporal Alexander F. Hubbell writes his mother from a bough shanty three miles from Strausburgh, electrified by a dispatch read to Generals Sigel and "Slow": Richmond captured after three days' fighting, thirty thousand men "left on the field." He prays Henry has "come out unscathed" and confesses he'll be ashamed to face his brother until he has seen two or three battles of his own.

author: alexander
old: Fourth of July 1862 — batteries firing, brigade harangued by Gen. Orders to move at moment's notice — leave tomorrow.
final: Independence Day, 1862, and Alexander marks it from Camp Goodrich near Strausburgh with batteries thundering and the brigade marched down to be harangued by Gen. Cooper. Orders have come to move at a moment's notice — tomorrow, he thinks, on a long march toward somewhere his Orderly guesses is Richmond. Yet beneath the soldier's bravado runs a son's worry: he is anxious for word of James, and gently scolds his mother not to believe "every old fogy" who steers her mail astray.

author: alexander
old: Fort Royal, VA — left Camp Goodrich July 5 at 5 PM, arrived 10 AM next day. Delayed by baggage trains.
final: Front Royal, Virginia — Alexander marches in safe and sound, the 60th NY pressing on from Camp Goodrich toward Manassas Gap, certain they're bound for Richmond. Beneath the soldier's swagger runs a brother's worry: he begs word of James, threatens to "pull" Frances's ears for her scraps of paper, and dreams that James will succeed so "we shall have one educated soldier in the family."

author: henry
old: SEVEN DAYS RETREAT firsthand. was in a battle the last of June.
final: Writing from a camp on the James River after a late-June battle and the army's retreat — "if we call it such" — Henry recounts flinging away his knapsack on the double-quick and watching the regiment's Major lose both feet to a solid shot, faulting the want of judgment that placed them under the rebel batteries. Yet his sister's plans have raised his spirits, and he now burns every letter he receives, slipping ten dollars into the envelope despite the risk.

author: henry
old: SEVEN DAYS RETREAT — extended detail. Sick ordered to hospital; McDonald came twice urging Henry to go; Henry stayed with the men.
final: Writing from camp near Harrison's Landing after the Seven Days' retreat, Henry recounts the double-quick into the woods, thrown knapsacks, and the bayonet charge where his regiment "fired very low and did great execution" — and the Irish Brigade storming a rebel battery, "a splendid sight, shouting at the top of their voices." Sick with worsening diarrhea, he twice refused McDonald's urging to go to the hospital, unwilling to leave the rest.

author: alexander
old: Literary landscape description — Virginia from Pine Mountain summit: "green fields, meadows, large farms, patches of woods, roads winding here and there, little villages.
final: On Pine Mountain near Warrenton, the twenty-year-old corporal watches the sun set behind the Blue Ridge, a bugle floating up, until he "almost forgot I was a soldier" — then imagines the drum beating to arms, the sun glistening on "ten thousand breastplates," and the earth that "will fairly rock." To Frances he confides a quieter ambition: when the war ends, college if he can — "I am determined to make something of myself."

author: alexander
old: "FIRESIDE PATRIOTS" — Silas and Sid: "brave enough at home. " "The idea of men at home finding fault while we are doing the fighting!
final: Two of her sons have proven themselves, Alexander tells his mother — and the letter shows the cost of that pride. Writing for the first time to Mother, Frances, and Charles at once, he scorns "fireside patriots" Silas and Sid: "brave enough at home, but let them come out here and you would see them whine." Then, the next morning, the First Lieutenant is dead, two more men buried, and Luther lies sick — disease, not battle, thinning the ranks.

author: james
old: JAMES AT WEST POINT — first extended description. Camp McRae on the plain.
final: James, just seventeen, writes brother Charles his first long account of life at West Point's Camp McRae, set on the plain and ringed by six sentinels who call "all is well" through the night. He renders the cadets' hazing with wide-eyed delight — wheelbarrows and an old cannon wheeled out to knock off bayonets; they dragged him about one night but never got his gun. Reading the Herald for word of McClellan, he confesses he was anxious for Henry until news came.

author: henry
old: GRAND REVIEW of Army of the Potomac at Harrison's Landing — "last Tuesday" (July 22). Near James River, within sight of gunboats.
final: Henry describes Tuesday's grand review of the Army of the Potomac near the James River — regiments marching in line of battle within sight of the gunboats, the battery firing blanks, an artist on hand whose sketch he expects in Harper's Weekly. Writing to his sister Frances, he confides a quieter wish: that peace might come "just before Sugar time" so he could farm again next spring, though he resigns himself to staying his time out — "there is no such luck for me." He signs off asking her to burn the scribble.

author: charles
old: CHARLES HUBBELL'S FIRST LETTER IN COLLECTION. Third brother to enter service.
final: Charles Hubbell enters the collection from the U.S. Barracks at Plattsburgh, where Dr. Foote nearly fails him for near-sightedness until a window-test of the lake shore lets the papers be signed — and Mr. Averill scolds him that he was "too honest." Within days he is appointed 1st Corporal, sleeping in straw-filled ticks on bunks four high, eating boiled pork and bean soup among "a good many hard cases" and a few decent men.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF ANTIETAM — September 17, 1862. The bloodiest single day in American history.
final: At Antietam two days after the bloodiest single day in American history, Alexander writes from "Camp on the battle field" to tell his mother he came through with only "an inconsiderable bruise a little below the right knee by a ball nearly spent." Then the pivot: "I only wish I could report the same of Henry," who is missing. A man of the 34th thinks him a prisoner, not killed, and Alexander builds careful hope. By a September 21 addendum, still no word: "Do not worry."

author: james
old: CHARLES ENLISTED — James just learned, wants details. Hopes not as private; advises promotion-seeking.
final: Charles has enlisted, and James — writing from West Point Academy on Sept 21, 1862 — has only just heard, pressing his mother for details: How did he enlist? Not as a private, he hopes, urging the boy to prove himself and seek promotion. Then the war recedes entirely: his rank in the third section, the prayer book Prof. French handed out, falling into ranks with shoes unblackened. "Ask Frances if she has forgotten me."

author: mother
old: FIRST HOME-FRONT LETTER IN THE COLLECTION. Mother writes Henry four days after Antietam, reading casualty lists with trembling, thanking God his name hasn't appeared.
final: Four days after Antietam, Mother reads the casualty lists "with trembling" and thanks God that Henry's name has not appeared, even as the 34th and Co. B are "terribly cut up." She begs for "the most minute things" from his own pen, confesses "if I was a man I am sure I should enlist," and grieves with Mrs. Carter over a fallen son — then closes, fatally certain the war is nearly over: "God bless McClellan."

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER HOSPITALIZED at Harpers Ferry. "Exhausting diarrhea for several weeks" combined with "severest military duty" — has "brought me pretty low.
final: Alexander writes from the Hospital at Harpers Ferry, brought "pretty low" by weeks of exhausting diarrhea and the severest military duty, yet softens it for his mother before the news she needs: Henry is alive, only slightly wounded in the hand, still with the company. Then the hard ask — could she spare five dollars, "if not, less will do." A loaf of bread bought by kind Orderly Dickinson "will do me a world of good."

author: mother
old: THE MOMENT MOTHER LEARNS. Between Sept 21 and Sept 28, Henry's name appeared on the published wounded list.
final: Henry's name surfaces on the published list of wounded, and his mother is undone: "I cannot tell you of the agony of mind I am in." Lacking only the means to fly to Washington, she begs Alexander to reach his brother, see to his every comfort, and secure a furlough so the two might come home together. She even asks whether she might come as a nurse. And tomorrow she must greet Charles, only to part with him too.

author: charles
old: Charles's first response to Henry's wounding. His theory — Henry is a prisoner at Richmond because the leg wound prevented escape — is a reasonable inference but unverified. He learned the news at 9 PM the previous night from "Alek Douglas." Expects to come home this week before mustering in.
final: Charles answers his mother from Plattsburgh Barracks with a young man's stubborn optimism: "it may be all for the best." Convinced his wounded brother Henry is a prisoner at Richmond, he reasons the leg wound only kept him from running — and that a prisoner is safer than a soldier. He learned of it at nine the night before, from Alek Douglas, while asking after the 34th regiment. He hopes to come home this week, once the men are mustered in together.

author: charles
old: Most detailed description of training camp life in the collection. Charles describes Plattsburgh Barracks in architectural detail: stone buildings, two-story, 6 rooms long, bunks 4 high and 6 deep, straw ticks and blanke...
final: Charles, three weeks a soldier at Plattsburgh Barracks, catalogs his new world like an architect: stone buildings six rooms long, bunks four high, sixteen men packed on an "elevator floor," and the wry confession that he's "only taken my pants off twice since I left home." Then Mother's letter arrives mid-page and the tone breaks: Henry, reported wounded in the thigh and taken prisoner. Charles clings to hope — "I think Henry is with the rebels in Dixie" — because alive beats the alternative.

author: mcdonald
old: THE ONLY OUTSIDE VOICE IN THE COLLECTION. McDonald, Henry's tentmate in the 34th NY, writes Mother Hubbell to report what he knows of Henry after Antietam.
final: McDonald, a stranger and Henry's tentmate in the 34th NY, writes Mother Hubbell from camp on Bolivar Heights to report what little he knows of Henry after Antietam: a flesh wound to the leg, ailing bowels, then nothing. His account of the 17th — "the sharp crack and whizz of the Rifle ball falling as thick as hail" — gives way to a chilling truth: only when the company calls the roll can anyone tell who has fallen. The only outside voice in the collection.

author: mother
old: MOTHER APPROACHES DESPAIR. She has received Alexander's Sept 19 letter (Henry missing after Antietam).
final: She received Alexander's letter of the 19th and wept with relief that he was spared "while thousands fell on your right hand & on your left" — but the same week brought only dread about Henry. McDonald reports him missing, DaValls examined the field and confirms it, and all agree he was wounded. Capt. Ransom takes tea in the parlor as she begs Alexander to get leave and search: "If he has gone, I must follow him soon."

author: mother
old: NEW EYEWITNESS REPORT ON HENRY. Young Fiser says: "Henry was seen to fall, that the rebels were within two rods of them, they fled, and know nothing more of him.
final: Yesterday's report from young Fiser has left Mother "half deranged" in Champlain: "Henry was seen to fall, that the rebels were within two rods of them, they fled, and know nothing more of him." She clings to another account that the field was searched and Henry not among the buried dead — proof, she prays, that he is a prisoner. To Alexander she prescribes the 91st Psalm and one ragged plea: "Write, write, write... WRITE."

author: charles
old: Charles returned from furlough to Plattsburgh. Received $25 check with $67 still owed. Double guards with loaded muskets to prevent desertion. Reports Alek Douglas's father severely hurt by falling timber. Still believes Henry is a prisoner. "Hoping that you & Frances will make the best of things."
final: Charles returns to Plattsburgh barracks to find double guards posted inside the fences, some with loaded muskets to stop his own regiment from deserting before payday. He sends two pairs of socks home with Alek Douglas, hurried off by his father's injury under a falling timber, and watches men burn $11 on beer the day a $25 check arrives with $67 still owed. He closes still clinging to the hope that his missing brother Henry is only a prisoner.

author: luther
old: Routine correspondence between comrades. Luther recovering at Eckington Hospital, wants news of the company. Capt. Ransom visited with items from home — the same Ransom who took tea at the Hubbell home in Champlain (Oct 2–3) and is now returning to the regiment.
final: Capt. Ransom came to the hospital ward yesterday, just back from Champlain, his arms full of the small comforts a sick soldier most needs. From his cot at Eckington Hospital in Washington, Amos C. Luther writes Alexander that he is mending fast from "a pretty long pull of sickness," aching for news of the boys and the regiment he means to rejoin. "I hardly know whether you are alive or not," he confesses — half jest, half dread.

author: charles
old: CHARLES'S REGIMENT IDENTIFIED: 153rd New York Volunteers, Company I. Detailed journey from Plattsburgh to Camp Mohawk near Fonda, NY.
final: Charles writes his mother from Camp Mohawk near Fonda, having marched from Plattsburgh through Whitehall, Saratoga, and Schenectady to join a regiment of 900 men where recruits sleep on straw "like so many pigs" and stealing is rife. He reports he's been appointed Corporal, settles family debts with the Savages, and frets over bounty disputes that nearly stalled the column. He's lost his razor — so he'll let his whiskers grow till he comes home.

author: mother
old: THE PRISONER THEORY DIES. Misner, returned from Confederate captivity, tells Mother directly: he and Albert saw ALL the prisoners taken at Antietam, and Henry was NOT among them.
final: Misner has returned from the South and dashed Mother's last hope: he and Albert saw all the prisoners taken at Antietam, and Henry was not among them. She fears now that he lies "one of the 'unknown' buried, or one of the number found in the bushes," yet cannot give him up — "I must hope against his end." Even congratulating Alexander on his sergeant's stripes, she begs: do not go into battle "without your name upon your person."

author: mother
old: FANNIE/FRANCES IDENTIFIED AS HUBBELL SISTER — signs "Aff. your sister, Fannie.
final: In uncertainty over Henry, Mother writes: "We are still in uncertainty with regard to Henry — it is terrible," yet still feels hopeful as letters from Mr. Vossey, Miss Cundia, and Ida Niles seem to have heard the worst. Fannie signs as Charles's sister, urging him to wear flannel across his chest; Mother's Tuesday postscript notes milk froze in the kitchen — "January weather." A rebel officer named Hubbell, glimpsed in a prison camp, hints at kin on the other side.

author: alexander
old: Alexander breaks a 46-day silence. After the hospital letter (Sept 27), his diarrhea evolved into jaundice, compounded by cold and a facial eruption threatening his eyesight. He has moved from hospital to Bolivar Heights to Harpers Ferry (guarding government property). He promises a longer letter when his eyes are stronger.
final: Alexander breaks a long silence from Harpers Ferry — "It is a long, long time since I last wrote you" — and the reason is a body unraveling: an indisposition that "took a permanent form in the shape of Jaundice," then a cold, then a facial eruption that left his eyes so weak he feared he would lose them. He writes only enough to ease his mother's worry, notes Capt. Ransom's great kindness, and promises a good long letter once his eyes are stronger.

author: charles
old: Most detailed account of garrison duty in the collection. 153rd NY guards Alexandria, the convalescent camp, parole camp, and provides funeral escorts. Two regiments guarding the city; countersign required after 9 PM. Corporals reduced to ranks for AWOL and threatening an officer (tied to telegraph pole). Death of a soldier from Fonda — company raised $72 for embalming ($50) and freight ($25). Charles is managing family property from camp: timber, cedar, Plummer's debt. Frances teaching French. Also reveals "Jones" = James (wrote to him at West Point).
final: Garrison duty near Alexandria fills this letter with the texture of a soldier's winter: two regiments holding the city, no passing after nine p.m. without the countersign, twelve cold hours at a post with no picket fires allowed. Charles's 153rd guards the convalescent and parole camps and furnishes funeral escorts — one sickly man from Fonda bled at the lungs and died, his company raising $72 to send his body home.

author: alexander
old: THE BROTHERS' REUNION. Alexander narrates finding Henry before Antietam — the only face-to-face meeting between the brothers described in the collection.
final: Alexander had begged the Colonel to let him slip the ranks, then walked alone by bright moonlight past every guard to find Henry's tent near Georgetown: "Is there a man among you by the name of Hubbell?" A large bearded man stepped out — "Why Dick, is that you?" — and their hands flew together. Writing now from Harpers Ferry, Alexander tells Mother he and Henry fought Antietam a few hundred yards apart, and clings to hope that Henry, wounded and "undoubtedly taken prisoner," still survives.

author: alexander
old: Alexander's most introspective letter. His description of feeling Mother's prayers during battle — "as tho I had a Mother upon her knees praying for me" while "shot and shell were shrieking and whirring around me" — is the collection's most vivid spiritual-combat passage. Thanksgiving on bean soup and hard tack while imagining Grandmother's dinner. Contempt for substitute-payers Whiteside and Doolittle. Government hasn't paid them; needs money again.
final: Alexander writes from Harpers Ferry that in the thick of battle, "while the shot and shell were shrieking and whirring around me," he felt "as tho I had a Mother upon her knees praying for me" — God's arm wrapped around him. Days later, on Thanksgiving, he pictures the "old castle," the pony's flying heels, and Grandmother's table while he eats bean soup, boiled pork, and hard tack from a tin plate. The Government still hasn't paid them; he asks, gently, for a little money.

author: charles
