old: Charles's first letter to Frances directly. Soldiers' cemetery description — "buried as close as possible in straight rows," headboards of "durable wood furnished by Government." Frenchman died, company couldn't raise money to send body home, buried in soldiers' cemetery. Lice prevention with unguentum. Thanksgiving on guard duty at a bridge. Mentions encouraging news about Henry from McDonald (details unclear) but doubts it: "too good to be true."
final: Charles writes his sister Frances from Camp near Alexandria, sketching the soldiers' cemetery where the dead lie "as close as possible in straight rows," each grave marked by a white headboard of "durable wood furnished by Government." A Frenchman from his tent has just been buried there, his company unable to raise the dollar apiece to send him home. Charles spends Thanksgiving guarding a bridge and clings to news of Henry he fears is "too good news to be true."

author: charles
old: Bounty system detailed — Charles breaks down his $67: $60 state, $28 county, $10 town, $2 enlistment fee. Fonda men received $200 town bounty plus $4/month. Self-inflicted wounds to avoid duty — two men shot fingers off "accidentally," another shot thumb and two fingers, another shot through arm. Exchanging Austrian rifle muskets for new guns. Band formed with soldier-bought instruments. Gen. Slough as military governor of Alexandria; Capt. Rich on his staff. McDonald to write his wife about Henry information.
final: Charles writes brother Alek from Camp near Alexandria, Va., still awaiting word that Henry, taken prisoner, will be exchanged and sent home. He itemizes his $67 bounty — $60 state, $28 county, $10 town, $2 enlistment fee — with pay three months overdue. Then the grim detail: four men have shot off their own fingers, thumb, or arm "accidentally," while Charles, who "did not enlist with the expectation of sleeping on a feather bed," guards Alexandria and waits for the war to close.

author: charles
old: McDONALD'S STORY CONFIRMED FALSE. Charles traces the information chain: McDonald → someone → Champlain → army friends → back to source.
final: McDonald's story about Henry could not be confirmed: Charles methodically traces the rumor back through Champlain, soldiers' letters, and paroled prisoners, concluding nobody can verify his brother is alive — "he may be a prisoner in some rebel hospital." Writing off guard from Camp near Alexandria, he records frozen creeks, a grave-yard fence burned for warmth, six months' pay owed, and a plea for woolen yarn and darning needles.

author: mother
old: McDONALD'S REPORT DEBUNKED. Mother now says "it turns out that McDonald has heard false rumor.
final: Henry is missing, and his mother conducts an investigation from her Champlain kitchen — "tell me who of 'the boys' saw him after he was wounded." She rejects McDonald's account as rumor, weighs Scott's report that Henry was seen on one knee two rods off, and fears he was buried by strangers like Dennis Hayes. By December 9, 1862, she pleads no longer for the war's end but for her son's life: "Can you get a discharge and come home. I cant live alone."

author: mcdonald
old: McDONALD REVEALS HIS SOURCE — AND IT'S A CHAIN OF HEARSAY. His information about Henry being alive came from Charles (of the 60th — i.
final: McDonald, an orderly sergeant of Co. D, 34th Regt. N.Y., answers a mother's plea to know whether her son Henry is dead or alive: word from Albert Cook at Annapolis, relayed by Henry's brother Charles of the 60th Regt., that Henry was taken prisoner with only a slight leg wound. He insists Henry could not have hidden after Antietam, for the woods stood clear of brush, the great trees set far enough apart to see a quarter to half a mile.

author: alexander
old: THE BEST EYEWITNESS ACCOUNT OF HENRY'S WOUNDING. Alexander visited the 34th NY camp and reports: "the boys said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and threw himself down.
final: Alexander, marching with cold-numbed fingers in a camp near Fairfax Station, sends his mother the eyewitness account she has waited for: "the boys said they saw Henry grasp his leg, take a step or two, and threw himself down." He clings to hope his brother lies in a rebel hospital. Six months unpaid and out of patience, he confesses he would sooner fight the abolitionists than the Southerners.

author: charles
old: ALEXANDER VISITS CHARLES — CHRISTMAS 1862. Alexander arrived by railroad from Fairfax Station (15 miles) on Christmas Day at 4 PM, left next morning at 11 AM.
final: Alexander rode the cars free from Fairfax Station to reach Charles's camp near Alexandria on Christmas Day, arriving at 4 p.m. and gone by 11 the next morning — long enough to split butter, currants, and ginger snaps between them. Charles notes his brother looks well but thin on rations, then turns to the tent's quiet truth: of twelve men only three can write, so he pens the others' letters, "what you have a mind to," since they tell him nothing to say.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER AT FAIRFAX STATION. Detailed description of Alexander's camp conditions: water from ditches, 60th NY called "the thieving reg't," $11 sutler debt, six months unpaid.
final: Charles writes from Alexandria, his company detached for straggler duty, ferrying soldiers back to their regiments by steamboat. The heart is his visit to brother Alek at Fairfax Station, where he found the 60th NY hard up: water drawn from ditches and mudholes, the unit nicknamed "the thieving reg't," Alek six months unpaid and $11 in debt to the sutler. Then he gently corrects his mother, who'd heard Henry was urged not to go into that fight: "every man was obliged to go."

author: alexander
old: Alexander's destitution put in perspective — he has been worse. "I have seen the time when I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night." March orders received evening of Jan 13 — 12 hours notice, "probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans." The religious commendation is notable: "We are all in God's hands."
final: Orders arrive at evening, and the letter pivots: "We have just received orders to be ready to march in twelve hours and are probably going east to reinforce Rosecrans." Hours earlier Alexander was all bravado, teasing his sister Fannie that nothing beats "a good hunk of raw pork with my hard tack" and shrugging off his destitution: "I have not had a shirt to my back or a blanket to cover myself with at night." Then, gentler: "Do not be troubled, Mother. We are all in God's hands."

author: james
old: OFFICER'S PERSPECTIVE ON THE HUBBELL FAMILY. Captain Ransom writes directly to Mother to reassure her about Alexander — "never looked so finely and well.
final: Captain James H. Ransom writes Mrs. Hubbell directly to ease a mother's "trying anxiety," reassuring her that Alexander "never looked so finely and well." He'd applied to send him home on recruiting service, then planned a furlough — until orders came to march at twelve hours' notice with eleven days' rations, destination unknown. A postscript catches the moment Charles arrives in camp to visit, "well and looks finely," before riding out at 7 the next morning.

author: charles
old: PAY RECEIVED — FIRST IN MONTHS. Two months' pay received; three more owed.
final: Charles writes his mother from Alexandria the very night the company is paid for two months, with three months still owed — and warns, dryly, that liberty in the city means "we will have some drunken men in our Co. for a few days." He encloses a $20 allotment check, then pleads against worry: "When I am not well I will let you know." A postscript finds him in a stone Episcopal church, the graves around it weather-worn and dated to the 1700s.

author: alexander
old: CAMP MOVED TO STAFFORD HOUSE. The 60th NY has marched from Fairfax Station to near Stafford House — closer to Fredericksburg.
final: Capt. Ransom has gone home on furlough — "much to my sorrow and the company's" — and Alexander had hoped to go with him, but Gen. Sigel refused to sign his application and sent it on to the War Department, where it may sit forever. Writing from a camp near Stafford House with no fire on a raw February day, he imagines what ten days' leave would bring: "I shall not know whether I am on my head or heals for the space of ten minutes." Rain floods the Virginia roads, and the army can only lie still.

author: charles
old: HOOKER'S ARMY REORGANIZATION. Pennsylvania reserves reduced from 15,000 to 2,300 — passing through Alexandria.
final: Charles writes his sister Frances from Alexandria that "Gen. Hooker's army is broken up," noting the Pennsylvania reserves went out 15,000 strong but have only about 2,300 left. He recounts guarding 200 stragglers to Aquia Creek, sleeping four to a steamboat floor with him in the middle for warmth, supping on hard tack and bean soup. Hoping to glimpse brother Alex with the 60th N.Y. nearby, he jokes about his beard and teases that Mother's been "converted into a Greclate."

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER GOT HIS FURLOUGH. The application denied by Sigel in early February was apparently approved by the War Department.
final: Alexander reached camp near Aquia Creek Landing safe and sound, six hours before his furlough expired, the journey from Rouse's Point to Washington costing $17.75 and forty-eight hours each way. Now the men are building fortifications. He urges his mother to keep a stout heart: "I believe this war cannot last much longer and trust I shall be home again soon."

author: charles
old: OFFICER CONFLICT IN 153rd NY. Armstrong resigned after difficulty with the Colonel, who is under arrest.
final: Lieut. Col. Armstrong, after falling out with the regiment's Colonel — now under arrest, Charles hears — has resigned, and came down to bid the company goodbye, promising to carry word home that Charles was all right. A man was buried yesterday, the fourth death here, though Charles assures his mother nearly all are well now. Between snow, mud, and his plea for two dollars toward knee-high boots, he keeps circling back to reaching Aquia Creek to see Alex.

author: alexander
old: POST-FURLOUGH REFLECTIONS. Alexander reliving his home visit in imagination.
final: A half-pint of whiskey ration arrives every day, and Alexander gives every drop away — "bound by a resolve I held most sacred in the world, a resolve to my mother." Writing from rain-stalled fortification work at Aquia Landing, where he oversees men raising earthen forts, he relives his recent furlough "all over again in my imagination," frets over a pony's hard ride to Rouse's Point, and tucks a torn dollar bill in the envelope, asking his mother to swap it for a whole one.

author: charles
old: 12-15 women living with husbands in the 153rd NY — drawing rations, washing clothes for pay. "A stout woman was marching through the mud after her husband.
final: Charles writes his mother from Alexandria, March 2, 1863, with a soldier's clear eye: twelve or fifteen women now live with their husbands in the regiment, each couple sharing a tent, the wife drawing rations and washing clothes for pay. He watches one stout woman marching through the mud after her husband — "our men thought she ought to stay at home." Unconvinced the war will end soon, he resolves to "stay my three years."

author: alexander
old: COMPLETE OFFICER TURNOVER IN CO. Ransom gone (Feb 6), both Lieutenants resigned — new Captain is Lieut.
final: New officers gone home and a new captain at the helm — Alexander writes from Aquia Landing that both his Lieutenants have resigned, leaving Lieut. Delany of Co. F as his new Captain, "a most excellent man — one after my own heart." Still building fortifications and "having jolly times," he teases his sister Fannie about a sleigh ride that badly frightened some poor Frenchmen, and promises to forward Cousin Mary McNeil's amusing political letter.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER AT AQUIA CREEK. Brothers meet again — Alexander "hearty as a buck," big fat face, pleased about furlough.
final: Charles writes from Alexandria, anxious that his mother's letters have stopped — three weeks waiting on two borrowed dollars for boots. He recounts a snatched visit to brother Alex at Aquia Creek: "hearty as a buck, big fat face," now third sergeant in the 60th, angling for a furlough he means to spend at home. Beneath the warmth runs unease — Aunt Laura has bought Henry's farm, and the men grumble that Capt. Ransom pocketed their ration money.

author: alexander
old: MAIL MISDIRECTION. Mother's letter with money for Charles (153rd NY) was misrouted to Alexander (60th NY) — postmaster confusion between regiments.
final: Mother's letter to Charles, with money inside, somehow reached Alexander instead — the postmaster crossing out "60th Regt." for the 153rd, then back again, before settling on the "sixtieth N.Y. Volunteers." Writing from Aquia Landing, where the forts are finished and the daily detail now unloads boats at the wharves, Alex forwards it on, sends Charles two pairs of socks, then turns somber at a paper from Mrs. Hoyle bearing notice of Dana Lyman's death.

author: charles
old: HENRY DEATH ACCEPTANCE ADVANCING. "I am afraid he was killed" — Charles's most direct statement yet.
final: Charles writes home from Alexandria, and tucked between a midnight fire he helped fight with Uncle Sam's new steam engines and a request for two borrowed dollars sits the letter's quiet heart: he has read in the Tribune that mothers can claim a pension for a son who is killed. "Savagham has never been heard from." A list of 400 Union soldiers dead in rebel hospitals is about to be published, and Charles urges his mother to see it.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S OPTIMISM PEAKS. Expects "honorable discharge...
final: Alexander writes from Aquia Landing on March 22, 1863, certain the end is near: "I expect, if I live, to be there in the course of ninety days with an honorable discharge in my pocket, and the war over." Between the teasing — Frances writing only "when the fit is upon you," Silas orating about hens and heifers — he recalls his mother boxing his ears during haircuts, calls his own writing "hen's tracks," and asks her to tell Miss Alma Mcyath she will soon fulfill her promise.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER REFUSES MOTHER'S PLEA FOR SAFETY. Mother asked Alexander to write the surgeon for "a place of safety in time of battle" — Alexander's response is fierce: "Would you have me branded as a coward?
final: Mother begged Alexander to write the surgeon for "a place of safety in time of battle," and from Aquia Landing his answer comes back fierce: "Would you have me branded as a coward?" Wherever his regiment goes, he will go. Yet the same hand admits, "Though I love my life as dearly as any one could love it," before turning homeward — to a restored Union, the spring sugar bush, and a certain tailor in Rutland he means to see.

author: charles
old: "I AM AFRAID THAT HE WAS KILLED. " Charles's second direct statement about Henry's death.
final: Charles writes from Alexandria, Va., and three times turns from camp life to the same dread: "Did Silas find out from that man at the Point about Henry. I am afraid that he was killed." Between asking after deserters in citizen's clothes and Lieut. Burdick — who "wore a streak of blue lightning" the night the long roll routed the camp — he tallies $2,500-a-ton hay, the rented-out farm, and 150 lbs. of maple sugar, a son quietly steadying his widowed mother while bracing her for loss.

author: charles
old: THIRD "I AM AFRAID HE WAS KILLED" STATEMENT. Charles now adds counterfactual: "If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in.
final: Charles writes from Alexandria that his regiment has just drawn new long Enfield rifles, their iron barrels blacked against rust, and he hopes they won't be ordered to scour them bright. Between target practice and marching three hundred stragglers a day from the convalescent camp, his mind keeps circling Henry: "If Henry had gone to the hospital when he was sick, he might have escaped some of the battles he was in. I am afraid he was killed."

author: mcneil
old: MICHIGAN PERSPECTIVE ON THE WAR. Cousin Mary from Atlas, MI: draft resistance, anti-emancipation sentiment ("sooner fight for the Union than to free the negroes"), high civilian mortality, truce hopes.
final: Cousin Mary, writing from Atlas, Michigan, finds the war pressing even on the home front: "considerable feeling" over the approaching draft, neighbors who would "sooner fight for the Union than to free the negroes," and a season so sickly two children were buried in one coffin. Charles wraps her letter in his own news — cannon booming in salute as Lincoln passes, a Lieutenant who ran when rebels took sixteen cars near Garrettstown, and the dry verdict that Vicksburg is not taken yet.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER STILL HOPES HENRY IS ALIVE. While Charles has said three times "I am afraid he was killed," Alexander clings to hope: "It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field.
final: Charles has said three times he fears Henry was killed, but Alexander still hopes: "It is singular that we can hear of no one who saw him dead upon the field." Writing from Aquia Landing under marching orders, eight days' rations packed, he calls Mother's fears "groundless and very foolish" — the cruelty of a man who cannot afford to grieve. Gen. Hooker, he says, means to give the two-years men "an opportunity to pay a parting salute to the rebels."

author: alexander
old: MAJOR MONEY TRANSFER. $40 by express + $7.
final: Alexander writes home from Aquia Landing, sending forty dollars by express and clearing his debts so the family need send no more — "I do not want you to lay this money up for me," he urges his mother. "Take what little comfort you can with it." A devoted soldier remembering camp under an apple tree and dreaming of showing her the drills at Montreal, he tucks in money for everyone, even worrying whether brother Jim wants for any.

author: alexander
old: HENRY'S CHARACTER FROM 34th NY COMRADE. A soldier from Henry's old regiment (34th NY) describes Henry's moral code: refused to take plundered goods — "the partaker is as bad as the thief.
final: A soldier from Henry's old 34th NY regiment passes along a comrade's portrait that pleased Alexander very much: when the boys went off plundering, Henry refused his share, reasoning "if I should take any, I would be as bad as any of you for the partaker is as bad as the thief." Quiet, seldom speaking unless spoken to, yet when bullied he would pitch into his tormentors with a will. Written from Aquia Landing, the note opens with a humbler want — a watch, double-cased.

author: charles
old: HENRY'S GRAVE MARKER REPORTED. Abram Fry (NY artillery) claims to have seen Henry's name on a headboard at his grave on the Antietam battlefield.
final: Abram Fry, an artilleryman, swore he had seen Henry's name on a headboard at his grave, but Charles weighs the claim and finds it wanting: "his story is very doubtful and there is no telling where he is now." Still, he concludes there is "not the least doubt that Henry was killed." Snowbound at Alexandria, he asks for two dollars for boots, encloses a $40 allotment check, and notes the 16th N.Y.V. shipping home from Sedgwick's Corps.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S FORMAL INQUIRY — THE ONLY LETTER FROM HER PEN IN THE COLLECTION. Hubbell writes to an unknown authority (possibly Sanitary Commission, military records, or hospital official) to trace Henry.
final: Frances M. Hubbell writes the only letter in her hand, a mother tracing her son Henry of Co. D, 34th N.Y., missing since Antietam, where he fell as the enemy charged and was never seen again. The surgeon swears every Union dead was identified and Henry not among them; the Colonel believed him taken to hospital. Yet she confesses a darker fear: she has read of soldiers held in an insane asylum at Williamsburg, Va., and dreads her nervous, feeble boy is among them.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S GRIEF — THE MOST EMOTIONALLY RAW DOCUMENT IN THE COLLECTION. Mother reads Henry's letters for the first time since his death — "I have wept until I am almost blind.
final: A widow reads her dead son Henry's letters for the first time since his death — "I have wept until I am almost blind" — recording his words: "I often dream of being home." McKee's letter now contradicts McDonald's claim that Henry limped away wounded, and Young Carter of the 34th, discharged after Antietam, reports Henry stood fourth in the ranks beside Ballerjy, who was killed. "My heart is breaking, breaking, breaking."

author: charles
old: CHANCELLORSVILLE CASUALTIES — 60th NY. 73 total: 9 killed, 43 wounded, 21 missing.
final: At Chancellorsville the 60th N.Y. lost seventy-three men — nine killed, forty-three wounded, twenty-one missing — yet Alexander writes that he missed the fight entirely, posted to guard the brigade trains while his regiment charged three times and drove the rebels back. Company H's one dead is named plainly: Lester Bond, shot through the forehead. He scorns the Eleventh Corps, which "broke and ran in a most cowardly manner," leaving the 60th unsupported.

author: charles
old: CHARLES SEARCHES FOR ALEXANDER AFTER CHANCELLORSVILLE. Went to Aquia Creek but couldn't find Alex — heard 60th was about a mile from landing.
final: Charles crossed to Aquia Creek to learn whether his brother Alex had come through the fight, only to be turned back by a Provost Marshal who would issue no pass — and never reached the 60th, posted a mile from the landing. He watched the war-worn 16th N.Y.V. ship home from Sedgwick's Corps, describing three rebel volleys in minutes, then confided his dread that Henry was surely killed. He encloses an ambrotype, his coat too large as always.

author: alexander
old: DETAILED CHANCELLORSVILLE CASUALTY LIST FOR CO. Brookway wounded; I.
final: Our regiment was pretty roughly handled at Chancellorsville, May 3rd — seventy-three lost, nine killed, forty-three wounded, twenty-one missing — yet what Alexander begs his brother Charley for, again and again, is a watch: without one he must guess the time when relieving his guards. He details Lester Bond shot through the forehead in a bayonet charge, and the 60th and 102nd N.Y. left unsupported, holding the enemy in check while the eleventh corps broke and ran.

author: charles
old: POST-CHANCELLORSVILLE REORGANIZATION. Burdick promoted to Captain; officer chain reorganized — Major to Col.
final: On a Sunday in Alexandria, expecting a cavalry raid, Charles watches Black men impressed off the street to throw up breastworks across every road to the wharves, where government stores wait — while his own regiment digs a defensive trench around the city. Word arrives that Alexander has come safely out of the fight, and Charles turns to an ordinary errand: sending $11.20 in greenbacks to buy his brother a watch. Burdick is back, promoted to Captain.

author: charles
old: CHARLES VISITS ALEXANDER — DETAILED CHANCELLORSVILLE AFTERMATH. Alexander was color bearer in the fight.
final: Charles crossed three lines of guards on the Alexandria wharf to reach Aquia Creek and surprise his brother Alexander with a $15 silver lever watch. Alexander, color bearer in the recent fight, told Charles he felt bad he could not stand with his regiment, having been detailed to guard a baggage train; Charles told him he was lucky. Back in Alexandria, contrabands were impressed on a Sunday to throw up stockades of green hardwood logs, eight to ten feet high, against an expected cavalry raid.

author: alexander
old: REDINGTON PORTRAIT — SINGING DURING SHELLFIRE. Alexander describes Col.
final: Lt. Col. Redington sang through the shellfire at Chancellorsville, Alexander tells his mother and sister — using "the screams of the shells as they passed over his head as a key to pitch his voice on," just as he had at Antietam. The slight, erect colonel is "a man of courage." Writing from camp near Aquia Creek Landing, Alexander signs off "in haste": June 4th orders have come to march with three day's rations, "probably merely a reconnoissance."

author: charles
old: "APPLY AT ONCE FOR HENRY'S BACK PAY AND BOUNTY. HE WAS KILLED, WITHOUT A DOUBT.
final: Charles writes from Alexandria of a magazine at Fort Lyons that exploded the day before, killing twenty and wounding as many a mile or two from his regiment's camp, a great noise still in his ears as he reports good health and easy swims in the Potomac. Then the harder business: "I think that you ought to apply at once for Henry's back pay and bounty." He was killed, without a doubt — file before the others do, or the family waits.

author: charles
old: Fragment only. Mother has left home to visit Charlotte. Frances is alone. June 29, 1863 — two days before the Battle of Gettysburg begins. Alexander's regiment is on the march.
final: Mother has left home for Charlotte, and Charles writes from Alexandria to ask the question that haunts the whole letter: "How do you get along alone and where are you staying?" He has had only two papers and one very short note since she left, and supposes she is still away — then the page ends mid-sentence. Dated June 29, 1863, two days before Gettysburg, this fragment catches a scattered family reaching across silence.

author: alexander
old: GETTYSBURG — FIRST-PERSON BATTLE REPORT. Alexander survived the Battle of Gettysburg without a scratch.
final: On Independence Day from a field near Gettysburg, Alexander Hubbell tells his mother that God has preserved his life through another terrific battle and he has not received a scratch — though his regiment lost fifty-two, eleven killed and forty-some wounded, in fighting that ran from 2 P.M. on the 2nd until midnight. He reports a great victory, then adds the day's grim work: "We are burying our and the rebel's dead today."

author: charles
old: July 4th grand parade in Alexandria — troops marched with whiskey rations. Charles hasn't heard from Alexander and doesn't yet know about Gettysburg. Henry's bounty application urged. Deserter caught through wife's letter — nabbed in St. Lawrence County.
final: On the Fourth of July the whole garrison at Alexandria paraded under the Brig. Gen'l. and his staff — sweat streaming, whiskey rations before and after, a speech almost no one could hear. Charles writes home unaware: "I should like to hear from Alex. Have not heard from him for a long time." A deserter from his own company sits in jail, betrayed when his wife's reply revealed his hiding place in St. Lawrence County.

author: alexander
old: POST-GETTYSBURG — TWO STANDS OF COLORS CAPTURED. The 60th NY captured two Confederate battle flags — a significant combat achievement.
final: Two stands of colors taken at Gettysburg, and seven rebel officers stretched out in a row before the company — Alexander writes his mother from near Crampton's Gap, having come through the battle "unscratched." The old 60th "beat the rebels gloriously," yet he braces for more: "We will doubtless fight tomorrow or next day. My life is in God's hands." Only miles from the Antietam ground, he hopes to find his brother Henry's grave.

author: charles
old: NEW YORK CITY DRAFT RIOTS referenced — "Don't you think New York has been a pleasant place to live in the last few days? " (July 13-16, 1863).
final: Writing from Alexandria a week after the New York draft riots, Charles asks his mother dryly, "Don't you think New York has been a pleasant place to live in the last few days?" The draft has delighted the soldiers — their one objection being the law letting drafted men buy their way out, since "$300 doesn't grow on every bush." Between worry over James after Hooker's forced march and a review in the hot sun, he recounts crossing the river for half a bushel of blackberries.

author: charles
old: Moved from Alexandria to Capitol Hill Barracks — detached from regiment for six months. Ration theft scandal — orderly sergeant, corporal James Lucas, and cook arrested. Col. very strict. Charles first learns Alexander survived Gettysburg through Mother's letter, not Alexander's.
final: Charles writes from comfortable barracks on Capitol Hill, his company detached from the regiment for six months after a sudden night move out of Alexandria — and confesses he only learned "Alex came safely out of that Gettysburg fight" from Mother's letter, never from Alexander himself. The mail had failed at the moment it mattered most. Meanwhile an orderly sergeant, a corporal, and the cook sit under arrest for stealing and selling ten days' rations the night before the march.

author: alexander
old: GETTYSBURG COMBAT DETAIL — P. provides vivid firsthand account: "fifty or sixty shots into the very teeth of the rebels.
final: At Camp near Warrenton Junction, Alexander Hubbell saves his fiercest news for the postscript: he fired "fifty or sixty shots into the very teeth of the rebels at Gettysburg," who charged "with hoots and yells" but "stopped their clack pretty quick." With the regiment down to about two hundred men, he cheers the draft, scorns those who got exempt — "Shame on their cowardly, craven hearts" — and asks his mother quietly for a little U.S. money.

author: alexander
old: Draft enforcement in Washington — citizens caught fleeing at R.R. Depot, young man arrested dressed as captain. Reg't guards two prisons and depot. James Lucas punished for ration theft (reduced to ranks, lost month's pay). Burdick resigned. Whiskey rations with quinine — antimalarial.
final: Charles, on guard at the R.R. Depot in wartime Washington, watches the provost's men arrest a boy of about nineteen fleeing the draft in a captain's coat too large for him — stolen or bought, he can't say. His regiment guards two prisons and the depot, James Lucas is reduced to the ranks for stealing rations, and each man is now marched to a hospital window for a daily whiskey ration he thinks is laced with quinine.

author: charles
old: Garrison life in Washington barracks — bed bugs, guard duty, draft enforcement. Charlotte visit suggested for Mother. Financial details — Savage debts, Surrogate office money, cow sale to Boyle. War assessment: "Jeff is about played out" but guerrilla fighting remains.
final: The draft has taken place — and from his Capitol Hill barracks, Charles tells Mother to "break up keeping house" this winter and go to Charlotte, gently proposing the end of the family home. His regiment guards two prisons and the depot while fifty men daily escort drafted conscripts from City Hall. He presses her to settle Savage's debts, and ventures a verdict: "Jeff is about played out, but there will be a good deal of guerilla fighting yet."

author: alexander
old: ANTIETAM BATTLEFIELD — ALEXANDER PASSED OVER IT. how I longed to leave the ranks and hunt for some trace of Henry, but it was impossible.
final: Marching through Maryland, Alexander passed over part of the Antietam battle ground — within half a mile of where he and the 34th had fought. "Oh! how I longed to leave the ranks and hunt for some trace of Henry, but it was impossible." Discipline held him in line, and he buries the loss between a joke about pulling his close-cropped hair and word that Sergt. Howes was reduced to the ranks for drunkenness.

author: alexander
old: "COULD YOU SUPPOSE I COULD EVER FORGET MY OLD HOME AND MY MOTHER? " Alexander's most emotionally raw letter to Mother.
final: Mother's letter wounded him before any rebel could: she feared he had forgotten her. "Could you for a moment suppose I could ever forget my old home and my Mother? Never, never," Alexander writes from Ellis Ford, blaming letters rifled beside the railroad. Across a hundred-yard river, he and the rebel pickets study each other "very composedly," past firing — "some of the Rebs are pretty nice fellows, much to my surprise."

author: charles
old: Garrison life — church services, library, bed bugs. James at West Point — 65 new cadets to fill southern vacancies. Burdick gone home. Methodist church incident — soldier drunk in church.
final: Garrison life at Capitol Hill Barracks: Charles writes Mother that his health is good, troubled only by bed bugs he's fighting with unguentine and hot water. He relays word from James — 65 new cadets to fill the West Point vacancies left by the seceded South. Then a Methodist church beside camp turns vivid: a soldier of his company shows up drunk, the ladies turn up their noses, and one man dubs it "a religious drunk."

author: charles
old: James's West Point demerits explained. Corporal died — sickness in regiment. Pet Steais hospitalized. Anecdote about soldier swindled by fiancée — $200 lost. Free library access.
final: James will get along well enough, his brother Charles guesses from Camp Davis on Capitol Hill, though he doubts the cadet will graduate high. Sickness runs through the regiment; a stout corporal of about twenty-one is suddenly dead, and Pet Steais lies in the hospital with something wrong in his chest. Then the garrison's dark comedy: an illiterate man who mailed his sweetheart his entire $200 in pay and bounty, only to learn she married another and spent it all.

author: alexander
old: EXECUTION OF DESERTERS — EYEWITNESS. Two men shot; one required three volleys.
final: A brigade execution of two deserters, witnessed up close: one man took three volleys to die, and both sat upon their own coffins beside open graves while every off-duty soldier was marched past to "learn a lesson." Alexander calls them "poor fellows" yet judges the killings "salutary," with five more men shot elsewhere that day. He notes it was the anniversary of Antietam, and braces for battle: "I am in God's hands and the thought gives me comfort."

author: charles
old: Garrison details. Pension advice — "with three sons in the army it looks bad." Alex Douglas likely to be discharged. Wife arrived at barracks — "What in hell did you come for!" James's demerits corrected. Mrs. Brikerhoff companion for Mother. Frances "teaches too constantly."
final: Charles writes from Capitol Hill with a soldier's eye for the small mercy: it is not his turn for the detail guarding prisoners out at 6:30 with three days' rations, "and I am glad of it, for the nights are cold and it might rain." Drill runs twice a day now. He urges Mother to refuse a pension: with three sons in the army, "it looks bad."

author: charles
old: ALEXANDER HEADING TO TENNESSEE — 11th and 12th Corps reinforcing Rosecrans (after Chickamauga). Alexander said "he did not care where they went, while they were riding they were not fighting.
final: The brothers meet by chance at a Washington depot — Charles falls out of dress parade to find Alex, only to watch the train pull a mile down the track to keep soldiers out of the city. Bound for Tennessee with the 11th and 12th Corps to reinforce Rosecrans, Alex is healthy, sunburnt, a moustache sprouting, weary of Virginia: "while they were riding they were not fighting." Charles had just guarded 282 ragged rebel prisoners down the Potomac to Point Lookout.

author: alexander
old: FIRST LETTER FROM TENNESSEE. Alexander at Murfreesboro as garrison.
final: Alexander's first letter from Tennessee is mostly mischief: he opens "I am highly provoked with you!" after Fannie dangled something "very, very funny" she dared not trust to paper, and threatens sweet revenge. His one nod to the war is wry — some Murfreesboro forts are built partly of cotton bales, "they do not use very extensively in York State for such purposes." A postscript adds the 60th N.Y. now garrisons the town under Gen. Greene.

author: charles
old: COLORED ODD FELLOWS PARADE in Washington — Black fraternal organization marching with uniforms, banners, band. Police present to protect them.
final: A grand parade of colored Odd Fellows marches through wartime Washington — uniforms, gay banners, a band, and women riding in coaches alongside white women, with policemen posted to keep them undisturbed. Charles records it from Capitol Hill in the same breath as Sunday sermons and a regimental school where many are learning to read and write. Then he turns geopolitical: if Rosecrans is defeated, he reckons it could be a seven years' war.

author: charles
old: BELLE BOYD — famous Confederate spy confined at Carroll Prison. Charles on guard duty when woman in broadcloth pants visited Boyd.
final: On guard duty at Carrol Prison, Charles watched a young lady in broadcloth pants and matching short frock stride past — the superintendent called her "Foster," joked about her breeches, and said women had no business in the army. She'd come to visit Belle Boyd, the confined rebel who flashes a small "secesh" flag at her guards. A soldier's eyewitness brush with two defiant women of the war.

author: charles
old: Furlough offered but declined — no money ($1.50). Election furloughs — soldiers going home to vote in NY elections. Cough/illness for a week. Money lost — $5 from vest pocket. Socks sufficient. Reg't singing "Let me kiss him for his mother." Steais in hospital again — breast complaint.
final: Charles declines a furlough home for the simplest reason in the war: he has only $1.50 to his name, having sent his pay to Mother in checks. Meanwhile, soldiers around him pack off on furloughs to vote in Tuesday's N.Y. elections. He reports a week's cough now mended, $5 jerked from his vest pocket and lost, five pairs of socks for winter — and, one night, the regiment serenading the Colonel with "Let me kiss him for his mother."

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF WAUHATCHIE (October 28-29, 1863) — Alexander's brigade attacked at night by Confederate forces. Greene seriously wounded — the hero of Culp's Hill at Gettysburg.
final: At Wauhatchie near Chattanooga, Alexander's company held a Cumberland Mountain pass that kept them out of the fight, while four miles off the rebels stormed the brigade at one in the morning, "barely alarmed before they were upon them." Brigade commander Gen. George S. Greene fell seriously, if not mortally, wounded. Pressed by Mother on a discharge, Alexander aches to return to his studies yet admits it would be hard "to leave the rest of the boys to fight it alone."

author: mother
old: SECOND MOTHER'S LETTER IN COLLECTION. Joy at receiving Alexander's Nov.
final: Word that Alexander's letter has come reaches Champlain like a reprieve — Mother had pictured him in Libby Prison, mangled in a field hospital, even among the "unknown" dead beside her lamented Henry, and his letter "quite overwhelmed us with joy." She begs him to shun "yellow covered" literature, keep his promise, and be a Christian soldier like Havelock. Yet she will set no Thanksgiving table: "How can I when all my boys are away! I cannot."

author: charles
old: 1,846 REBEL PRISONERS transported to Old Capitol prison — reg't up all night. Some taken to Point Lookout.
final: 1,846 Confederate prisoners arrived near morning, and Charles's regiment — up all night at the Washington depot — marched them with cavalry to the Old Capitol prison, a heavy detail later moving some to Point Lookout. He counts himself lucky to have missed both. Writing his mother from Capitol Hill, he weighs selling the house and notes those who went home to vote had their fare paid by New York's Union party — news that reached him too late.

author: charles
old: $18.78 stolen from pocket book — someone found it with money, returned it empty. $20 check enclosed for Mother. Clothing account settled — $2.70 surplus from $42/year allowance. Col. trying for Philadelphia; may go to Alexandria or Chattanooga. New guns replacing old ones.
final: $18.78 vanished from a soldier's pocketbook: lost beside the knife he'd pulled from the same pocket, then returned with the check intact but the money gone — "they found it without any money in it." From Capitol Hill, Charles encloses a twenty-dollar check for his mother yet must ask her for $2, begging she "not tell all creation." Rumors swirl of orders to Philadelphia, Alexandria, or Chattanooga, and the regiment is trading good guns for new.

author: alexander
old: DISCHARGE EFFORT — CAPT. RANSOM INTERCEDING.
final: Capt. Delaney calls Alexander into his tent to relay a discharge plea from Capt. Ransom — but the surgeon and colonel have no power to grant it. Alexander, with eleven months left to serve, sees the futility plainly: "Secretary Stanton is the man to apply to, or else the President." Writing from muddy Wauhatchie, he humors his mother's hope even as Gen. Geary marches them out under arms in the rain for no purpose but speed.

author: alexander
old: WOUNDED AT LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN — "BATTLE ABOVE THE CLOUDS" (November 24, 1863). Alexander hit by minie ball in left side — "rather a close call for my life.
final: Wounded at the storming of Lookout Mountain, Sergeant Alexander F. Hubbell writes Mother from the General Hospital at Tullahoma: a minie ball in his left side, "rather a close call for my life." Even bleeding, he files Company H's casualties in orderly rank — George Hays killed; himself, Long, Ish, Kelly, and Sidney Rider wounded. The rebs "ran like good fellows," surrendering 1,800 prisoners. "God has been very good to me. I shall soon be back to the regiment."

author: charles
old: Charles aware of Chattanooga fighting — "Hooker's fight" — but doesn't know Alexander was wounded. Half rations. Pocket book saga continues — check system explained in detail. Thanksgiving dinner: mashed potatoes and milk gravy. Milk women selling at 10¢/qt.
final: Charles writes from Capitol Hill, anxious for word of his brother: "I should like to hear how Alex came out of Hooker's fight, but I don't borrow trouble as it does no good." Around that worry he heaps the small comforts of an easy winter — johnnycakes and butter bought with company savings, milk at ten cents a quart, mashed potatoes and milk gravy for Thanksgiving — and the long, careful saga of a pocket book picked at dinner, its stolen check now traceable through the paymaster.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S AGONY — DOES NOT KNOW IF ALEXANDER IS ALIVE. Oh, where are you?
final: Mother does not know if Alexander is alive. "Where are you? Oh, where are you? Not a word have I heard since the late battles in Tennessee" — she shrinks from the "long dark catalogues" of the dead at Lookout Mountain, dreading Belle Island, while Henry's loss rises beside her fear for the living. Practical still, she prices his shirts and boots, then signs herself "Anxious and affectionate Mother."

author: charles
old: Garrison routine — Carroll Prison guard duty resumed. Union church formed — all denominations, mostly Methodist. Congress in session — Charles plans to attend. Gen. Slough's "band box regt." Theater passes. Still no news from Alexander after Lookout Mountain.
final: Garrison duty resumed: Charles's regiment took over guarding Carroll Prison again, relieving the Invalid Corps, and now expects to winter in Washington — relief, he notes, that "nobody is sorry" about. He writes with a soldier's dry eye, recalling their nickname as Gen. Slough's "band box regt." for the five-cent collars, and plans to walk two blocks to hear Congress in session. Of his brother Alex, still unheard from, he refuses to "borrow trouble, as that doesn't pay."

author: alexander
old: COMPREHENSIVE BATTLE NARRATIVE — WAUHATCHIE, LOOKOUT MOUNTAIN, MISSIONARY RIDGE, RINGGOLD. Alexander recounts the 60th NY's engagements since arriving in Tennessee.
final: Climbing Lookout Mountain under enemy fire, Alexander tells his brother Charley the soldier's version: hauling himself up the steep slope by hand, "which you know, in the face of the enemy is not over pleasant." The 60th opened the road to Chattanooga with Hooker, thrashed Longstreet, then made a grand bayonet charge that sent the rebels running and took 1,800 prisoners. His own wound spared him Missionary Ridge and Ringgold — but not the company's toll: Majo, Doten, and Housedean killed.

author: alexander
old: Alexander back with regiment — left hospital early. Side still sore. Half rations — supply problems. Confirms Co. H losses at Missionary Ridge and Ringgold: Doten and Housedean killed, Lemage and Small wounded (Small lost leg). Sergt. Long confirmed unhurt. Expects to move soon.
final: Alexander writes from his old camp at Wauhatchie that he has rejoined the regiment and is doing duty, though his side is "still pretty sore" — he had quit the hospital early, telling the surgeon he was ready, his wound having made him miss Missionary Ridge and Ringgold. He sends the loss of Company H: Doten and Michael Housedean killed, Lemage and Thomas Small wounded — Small's "leg torn off." The army is on half rations, "Old Bragg" near used up. He closes by the last of his candle.

author: charles
old: New Year's and Christmas celebrations — turkey dinner, lager beer, flour pudding. Re-enlistment bounties — $1,000 for three years; Charles advises Alex not to re-enlist. Marching orders to Harper's Ferry countermanded. Turkey theft. Geo. Dodds visited from hospital.
final: Christmas dinner in camp on Capitol Hill ran to eight turkeys, two kegs of lager, and a bread pudding bought with company funds — though Charles, who dislikes beer, watched the boys get "quite happy" while one drunken Irishman was carried in "as if he had been a dead pig." Marching orders to Harper's Ferry came and were countermanded by morning; Charles, weighing the $1,000 re-enlistment bounty, urges Mother that Alex had better not sign on again.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER RE-ENLISTED AND LEFT DETACHMENT "CLANDESTINELY. " Technically reported as a deserter — but deserted his detachment to rejoin his regiment.
final: Alexander writes from a Nashville hotel, "on my way to Savannah to join the regt." — and to get there he had to slip out of Chattanooga "clandestinely." "I suppose I am reported at my detachment as a deserter, but this will do me no harm." A sergeant deserting a rear-area post to rejoin the fighting, smuggled through with a detachment of the 18th Corps bound for Sherman. Then the mask slips: "I feel quite sad tonight... Frances would say that I have the blues."

author: charles
old: REGIMENTAL SCANDAL. Davis and Adjutant under arrest — court martial for bucking and gagging, trying to remove U.
final: Davis, the regiment's colonel, and his adjutant sit under arrest at Capitol Hill — court-martialed for bucking and gagging the men and for filing the U.S. mark off a government horse, while a false muster at Fonda enrolled the same soldiers in two or three companies to draw bounty for men who never served. Charles tells his mother the men still like Davis and dread losing him. Quieter but historic: Corporal Trombly of his company has won a commission as 2nd Lieutenant in a colored regiment.

author: charles
old: Guard bribed $200 to let prisoner escape — sentry in prison, rumor he will be shot. Charles attended Congressional debate on confiscation — Democrat vs. Republican. Love feast in church — soldiers attending for girls. $450 town bounty discussion. Sidney's family trouble.
final: A guard in Charles's regiment took a $200 bribe to free a prisoner who was recaptured fleeing the city — and now, Charles writes from Capitol Hill, the rumor is the sentry will be shot. He fills the rest with a soldier's wry eye: the most profane man in his company taking communion bread "for the congregation," three comrades who attend church only to see the ladies, and an afternoon spent listening to Congress debate confiscation, Democrat against Republican.

author: charles
old: POINT LOOKOUT PRISONER CAMP. Charles escorted ~400 rebel prisoners to Point Lookout — camp holds ~8,000.
final: Charles writes from Capitol Hill, where his regiment now stands four reliefs deep — two hours on post, the guard never changing because there aren't enough men to relieve it. A week earlier he had marched with a hundred others to Point Lookout, escorting nearly 400 rebel prisoners to a camp of 8,000 penned behind an eight-foot board fence, sentinels pacing a walk near its top. He worries over Alex's bounty and dreads the thought of young James enlisting at all.

author: charles
old: LEAVING WASHINGTON FOR ALEXANDRIA. Sudden orders — regiment relieved from guard duty.
final: Sudden orders, written in haste on the coldest day of the winter: Charles tells his mother the regiment leaves Capitol Hill for Alexandria at 7 the next morning, with no one sure whether they march or take a steamboat, or whether the destination is Texas or the Army of the Potomac. He encloses a $20 check and $10.60 in greenbacks, having sold his double-cased watch for $17.50. "I hope you will not worry about us boys. Everything will come out all right."

author: alexander
old: Transit through Nashville — visited Thos. Small at hospital, lost leg at Ringgold. Luther's bounty spending. Comfortable passenger cars instead of freight cars.
final: Alex F. Hubbell, in plenty of leisure on a brief transit halt at Nashville, takes a pass into the city and finds Thos. Small in hospital No. 8 — one of his own wounded boys, who lost his leg at Ringgold and now seems "doing well and very cheerful." Even the cars surprise him: comfortable passenger seats instead of the cold freight cars they'd expected. Then, in the same breath, he asks his mother whether Frances and the others have been down to the ravine to slide.

author: alexander
old: REBEL CAPTAIN CONVERSATION — Confederate conscription: "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts.
final: A rebel cavalry captain Alexander spoke with at Stephenson, Alabama let the Confederate collapse slip in his own words: "they send a whole regt. of cavalry to guard half a dozen conscripts." On a hushed Sabbath morning — birds singing, the war momentarily still — he and his tent mates refused to build their shanty, certain that soldiers above all needed God's blessing. Across from camp lay the Chickamauga dead, and a defiant reb warned, "wait until the next fight and you will be prisoners."

author: alexander
old: Confederate hasty evacuation — guns left unmuzzled, carriages burned, enormous rifled guns on track. Kilpatrick's raid disrupted railroads. Sherman on the move. 60-mile march to reach this location. Immense ordnance abandoned.
final: At Charleston, Tennessee, Alexander reaches camp after a sixty-mile march and walks the abandoned Confederate forts. He finds guns left unmuzzled and "fit for immediate use," two gun carriages burned, and a pair of enormous rifled guns lying beside the track, ready for cars that never came — Kilpatrick having torn up the railroads first. "The Johnnies must have left here in considerable haste," he tells Mother, with Sherman already off again and no telling when they'll catch him.

author: charles
old: 153rd NY ARRIVES IN LOUISIANA. Sea voyage from Alexandria via steamship Mississippi — entered Mississippi River mouth on 4th day.
final: Charles writes his mother from Algiers, across the river from New Orleans, after the 153rd New York's steamship Mississippi voyage from Alexandria, entering the river mouth at daylight one Sunday morning to find sugar plantations, orange groves, and darkies tossing oranges that fell short of the boat. His regiment now quarters in a smashed-windowed iron works with no floor but the bare ground. Rumor has it an expedition is fitting out for Mobile.

author: charles
old: CHARLES DETACHED AS CLERK AT GEN. Mother's letter-writing campaign succeeded — Mrs.
final: Mother's quiet campaign finally lands her son a desk. Writing from Gen'l. Banks's New Orleans headquarters on March 6, 1864, Charles thanks her plainly — "you are at the bottom of this matter" — after she wrote the Surgeon and Mrs. Strain pressed her husband to detail him as a clerk, the Lieut. Col. having refused to spare "so healthy a man." Safe in a third-story office as his regiment marches toward hard fighting, Charles confesses his copying still falters: "I wish I understood punctuation."

author: alexander
old: REBEL DESERTERS' TESTIMONY. Johnson's army suffering for food — one day's ration scarcely enough for one meal.
final: Rebel deserters from Johnson's and Longstreet's armies paint a doleful picture: rations barely enough for one meal in a day, men determined not to stand at the next fight, and the admission that "the Confederacy was played out and that it was only the pride of the leaders that kept it up." Writing from Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander also appoints his mother and Frances his "business agents in Champlain," trusting the women at home to chase down his bounty money.

author: alexander
old: Personal letter to sister. Playful tone. Yearning for civilian life — "the proudest day of my life."
final: He warns his sister Frances against flattery with a mock-pompous flourish — a philosopher so busy walking with his head among the stars that he tumbles into a ditch and breaks his neck. Yet beneath the play runs a soldier's ache: writing from Stevenson, Alabama on March 7, 1864, Alex longs for the day he can lay aside "the terrible title of a 'veteran soldier'" and walk among friends as a citizen — "the proudest day of my life." The brigade band practices nearby, the music grand.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S MOST LITERARY LETTER. Vivid panoramic description of camp — picket fires, earthworks, brass battery gleaming, Brigade band, drums, Guard Mounting, dinner call, dress parade, Tattoo, Taps.
final: Camp at Stevenson, Alabama, and Alexander finally makes good on a long-promised letter to his sister Fannie — though picket duty and an order to guard prisoners at Chattanooga keep interrupting the writing. What he offers her is a word-painting of a beautiful day: distant picket fires, a brass battery glistening on an earthwork, the Brigade band, and Taps, "the last plaintive, soothing call of the bugle." His scorn for the Southern sympathizers back home is just as vivid.

author: charles
old: RED RIVER CAMPAIGN — victories at Fort DeRussy and Alexandria reported. Fox dismissed for disloyalty and conduct unbecoming.
final: A woman steps onto the streetcar track to watch a passing Military Company, panics at the mule too late, and is run down — left under a piece of old carpeting awaiting the coroner: "She was a poor, white woman," Charles writes from Headquarters at New Orleans. He reports the army's Red River victories at Fort DeRussy and Alexandria, then notes Capt. Fox of his regiment dismissed for disloyalty and conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.

author: alexander
old: Warrant renewed — old position in 60th Veterans. Marching orders for Chattanooga or Knoxville. Requests boots and stamps.
final: Warrant renewed — a mere formality — and Alexander holds his old position in the 60th Veterans again. But the real news is in the marching orders: he leaves Stevenson, Alabama in a few days for Chattanooga or Knoxville. Beneath the soldier's business runs a son's ache — no letter came that morning, and he was "very much disappointed." He asks twice for word from home, after his brothers James and Charles, and confesses he is entirely out of stamps, borrowing to send this.

author: charles
old: Charles's comfortable clerk life at Banks HQ — sleeping on office floor with marble mantle and washstand. Extra pay $11 for first month. Banks and staff in the field (Red River). Roses blooming in March. Red River Campaign — "expect to clear rebels out."
final: At Department of the Gulf headquarters in New Orleans, clerk Charles reports $11 in extra pay he insists he hasn't earned — "I have done hardly anything." He sleeps on the office floor of a carpeted, third-story room with a marble mantle and a marble washstand fed by a spigot, knapsack in the corner, while Banks and most of his staff are in the field on the Red River, where the troops "expect to clear the rebels out." Roses are already in bloom in a city park.

author: alexander
old: 20TH ARMY CORPS FORMED — 11th and 12th Corps consolidated under Hooker. Slocum to Vicksburg.
final: Marching orders read at parade leave Alexander stripping for the coming campaign — surplus baggage to the rear, his overcoat sent off, with one grim line: "We shall probably have a hard summer." But his anger burns hotter at home, where twenty-five Champlain men voted against letting soldiers vote: "Whoever did deserves to be blasted with eternal infamy." A 6 P.M. postscript records the mail's arrival and no letter — "I fear all is not right at home."

author: alexander
old: BASEBALL IN THE CIVIL WAR — "UNION BASE. " Two regiments challenged the 60th NY to a game of "Union Base" — a kind of game of ball.
final: The 60th NY met two regiments of the Brigade in a game of "Union Base," a kind of game of ball, and beat them badly — soldiers at leisure before active service, with a fiddle and a grand dance on the company street. Alexander catalogues the camp's amusements: a horse race, greased pole, and a greased pig loosed for the contrabands. "A letter of ten pages. Beat it if you can."

author: charles
old: RED RIVER CAMPAIGN BATTLE REPORT — "terrible fighting in western Louisiana" — victory "so bloody we were not able to take advantage of it. " 153rd NY was in it.
final: Charles writes from Department of the Gulf headquarters in New Orleans, copying down the official word on "terrible fighting in Western Louisiana" — a victory "so bloody that we were not able to take advantage of it." The 153d was in it; he doesn't yet know its losses. Then a clerk's drunken death: a head-first pitch over a third-story banister onto the stone pavement. "He never saved nor groaned."

author: alexander
old: JAMES HAS ENLISTED. Alexander assesses James's chances — doubts cavalry, thinks he'll rise to straps (officer).
final: From his camp at Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander weighs his youngest brother's prospects with a veteran's eye: he doubts the cavalry story and a commission from Gov. Seymour, but is sure James "will surely rise in the service — I do not mean to stripes but straps." He watches Gen. Thomas, "a tremendous large man" with a snow-white beard, review the troops, then pities six Indiana regiments straggling in "poor and haggard." "Few men at the north have any idea of what a soldier has to endure."

author: alexander
old: 20TH ARMY CORPS ORDER OF BATTLE. Complete brigade composition listed.
final: Alexander writes Mother from Stevenson, Alabama, the day his unit is "at length fully organized" into the 20th Army Corps, Army of the Cumberland — and recites the order of battle by heart so she can "give an intelligent answer to any one who may inquire about the Corps." Then the guard drops: though he has tried to call McClellan's removal a good move, "I cannot do it. My heart still yearns toward the man." A soldier confessing the general he still loves.

author: charles
old: CHARLES RELIEVED FROM HQ — RETURNING TO REGIMENT. Penmanship not good enough.
final: Charles writes his mother from New Orleans, relieved by Special Order on April 21st and ordered back to his regiment massed on the Red River, where "another fight" is expected soon. He'll carry the mail to Gen. Banks's headquarters by boat — "a long ride up the Red River which is better than footing it the way the army did." Between reassurances about his brothers, he turns tourist: wooden cisterns tall as houses, sidewalks called banquettes, mule-drawn streetcars run on the honor system.

author: charles
old: BROTHER-TO-BROTHER LETTER — rare front-to-front correspondence. Expanded clerk death account — burial scene with wagon of 8 bodies, clerk's prayer, volleys, streetcar home.
final: From New Orleans, Charles writes his brother Alex of a clerk who came in drunk at midnight, pitched headlong over a third-story gallery rail to the stone pavement below, and never moved — buried beside a wagon of eight bodies, a clerk's prayer standing in for the absent chaplain, the volleys fired, "and we got into the street car and came home." Relieved of headquarters duty for poor penmanship, he's bound up the Red River to rejoin Banks's army.

author: alexander
old: EVE OF ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — ALEXANDER'S FAREWELL. "It is the death struggle of this mighty rebellion.
final: The Atlanta Campaign opens with a soldier's quiet goodbye. Bound for the front from Stevenson, Alabama, Alexander tells Mother battles are coming within weeks that may "throw completely in the shade" Antietam and Gettysburg: "It is the death struggle of this mighty rebellion." He braces her for the worst, then softens it with talk of letters owed and boots not yet arrived, asking only that she not worry — and sending love, particularly to Frances.

author: charles
old: GUERRILLA WARFARE ON RED RIVER. Steamer fired upon — 1 killed, 1 wounded on boat.
final: On the Red River above Alexandria, the clerk-turned-soldier finally fired his gun in anger—from behind a breastwork of hardtack boxes—as guerrillas raked the steamer with musketry and a rebel cannon was dismantled by the gunboat. One man was shot dead on board, another wounded, with bullets striking near where Charles crouched. Most haunting: three soldiers who chased cattle ashore never returned. "The boat whistled and waited," but they were gone, supposed shot or taken by guerrillas.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — FIRST LETTER FROM GEORGIA. "Close upon the enemy.
final: Alexander's first letter from Georgia opens the Atlanta Campaign — "We are close upon the enemy. Our advance came upon them this morning but they fell back." Writing from "Camp somewhere in the State of Georgia," he reckons 35,000 to 40,000 men under Hooker, his regiment on the army's extreme right. The boots his mother sent were too small for his "used up feet," so he sold them and drew government bootees. He signs off as the mail leaves: "Keep a stout heart."

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — ALTOONA CREEK. Alexander in Georgia, still safe.
final: Three Hubbell brothers are in combat at once, and Alexander — writing from Camp near Altoona Creek, Georgia, as the mail leaves "in a few minutes" — knows only that James faced "terrible fighting in Va." and prays he and Charley are safe. He reports himself well and just two men of Co. H injured, then asks his mother to find him on the map in Cobb Co. and send stamps. "If there is any one that needs God's help," he writes, "it must be a soldier."

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF BUZZARD'S ROOST / ROCKY FACE RIDGE. Detailed tactical account — 1st & 2nd Brigades engaged, 3rd Brigade on cavalry support reconnaissance.
final: Buzzard's Roost was a high rocky ridge reachable only through a narrow gap, and Alexander's 3rd Brigade missed Sunday's fight, drawn off to support a cavalry reconnaissance. He describes rebels behind rocks and ledges firing "such a withering fire" that the 1st and 2nd Brigades could only hold long enough to remove their wounded — leaving the dead — then fall back, attacks he judged feints. Reading that the Army of the Potomac had driven the rebs ten miles, Sherman told the troops "let us do likewise."

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF RESACA (May 13-15, 1864). Alexander came through unscathed.
final: At Resaca on Sunday the 15th, the troops went in "in a way that I never saw before being formed in solid column," under heavy fire from eleven A.M. until long after dark. Alexander writes his mother that he came through unscathed — and that owing to the ground, a succession of ridges, "not a man of Co. H was hurt." He would rather tell her in person, which he trusts will not be long. The enemy is defeated; they are in close pursuit.

author: alexander
old: BASS SHOT — probably fatally. The schoolteacher/Southern sympathizer from Champlain has been shot (by Dodds?
final: Mr. Bass has been shot in Champlain, "probably fatally" — Alexander reads it in a paper while resting in Camp near Kingston, Georgia, pursuing Johnson's army. "I think Dodds must have been deranged. Who will now teach the old Academy?" The war at home collides with his own: a brutal comrade picks up a severed rebel leg and shakes it in their faces, and Alexander wants to knock him down with his gun butt. The eastern men, he notes, are learning to respect the Star Corps.

author: charles
old: JAMES HUBBELL ARRIVES — JOINS CHARLES'S REGIMENT. Three brothers now confirmed in active service.
final: James Hubbell walked into Charles's tent on May 23rd, 1864 — the surprise of a younger brother arrived by transport from New Orleans to enlist in his very regiment, where the two will now tent and draw rations together. Charles describes the brutal march from Red River, half a day in line of battle as cavalry skirmished ahead, and a Colonel's news that Richmond had fallen, met with lusty cheering. Along the road he passed Mother's own letters, captured by the rebels and scattered in the mud.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF DALLAS / NEW HOPE CHURCH (May 25-June 4). Writing under fire — "there goes one now — b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l.
final: Writing under fire from the entrenchments near Dallas, Georgia, Alexander reassures his mother he is "all right thus far" even as bullets whistle overhead — interrupting his own sentence to admire one passing: "there goes one now — b-e-a-u-t-i-f-u-l." He reports James Thurber and John Rawlins of Co. H wounded, the regiment's loss at twenty-eight with seven killed, and the rebel works so close they can hear the enemy talk. He asks only for postage stamps and a silk handkerchief.

author: charles
old: JAMES HUBBELL — LANCE CORPORAL. Already promoted, drilling recruits.
final: James Hubbell has been made Lance Corporal — acting as corporal, drilling the recruits — and Charles reports it with a brother's quiet pride from their shared camp at Morganza Bend on the Mississippi. He enlisted March 9th in New York City as a farmer of Champlain, Clinton Co., never showing his papers from the West Point officers, and drew an $860 bounty. Between the news, Charles cooks his own rations: pancakes of flour, water, and salt, fried heavy but good.

author: alexander
old: SIX LETTERS FROM HOME after weeks without mail. Bass recovering — shooting described humorously.
final: Six letters from home at once, and Alexander is "jolly" — the mail drought breaks at Marietta as the army rests before chasing the Johnnies, who have "dug out" toward Atlanta. He teases Mother's lurid account of Mr. Bass's shooting — "I have seen thousands of men wounded but hardly ever say anything come up to the pail of blood" — then tallies bounties and loans, hoping to send home over $600. One small ask closes it: please send a silk handkerchief.

author: charles
old: Foraging expedition — 15 miles, two regiments, wagon train. Corn taken from barns — women objected. Money sent home: Charles $50, James $330, Joseph Martin $20 for wife. James's bounty details. Pay increase rumor — $16/month from May 1.
final: Foraging fifteen miles out with two regiments and a long wagon train, the men pried the side boards off Louisiana barns and loaded the wagons with husk-on corn; Charles notes only that "the women did not like to see the corn taken." Writing Mother from camp on the Mississippi at Morganza, he tucks $400 into an express package — $50 his, $330 James's bounty pay, $20 a Frenchman named Joseph Martin asks be carried to his wife in Champlain.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — NEAR MARIETTA, APPROACHING KENNESAW MOUNTAIN. Fighting nearly every day.
final: Alexander writes his mother from a camp near Marietta, Georgia, with the 60th N.Y. Vets, having fought nearly every day and entrenched every night for a week. "The list of killed and wounded in our regt. is beginning to pile up fearfully," he reports, having skirmished the Sabbath from two P.M. until after ten. He twice begs for a silk handkerchief, then leaves his testament: how little the North realizes what the country has cost — it "ought to be prized beyond rubies after this is over."

author: james
old: JAMES HUBBELL'S FIRST LETTER. The youngest brother writes for the first time in the collection.
final: James Hubbell's first appearance in the collection finds the youngest brother encamped at Morganza, Louisiana, fresh off his single trial of marching — a foraging run that loaded one hundred wagons from a French woman's farm while soldiers were forbidden to take so much as a chicken. He notices everything: negroes speaking French like their masters, sugar mills that yield a spoonful a day. To Frances he turns almost shy — "What do you think of this war?"

author: charles
old: Brief note appended to James's letter. Dr. Sweeney — saw Frances recently. Express charges: $4 freight + $2 insurance on $400.
final: Dr. James Sweeney, the new Assistant Surgeon, sent a boy to fetch "the two Hubbells" to his tent — the Champlain network reaching all the way to a Louisiana camp. He'd seen Frances three weeks before and was glad of the company; the regiment had gone without a second surgeon since leaving Washington. Charles closes with a bookkeeper's note: $4 freight and $2 insurance on the $400 sent home by express.

author: charles
old: Camp economics — butter, flour, dried apples, pies, doughnuts. James making doughnuts (heavy — no yeast powder). New York papers 25¢. Chaplain says won't stay long — garrison somewhere near Mississippi.
final: James yesterday made his first attempt at doughnuts — frying the grease out of a lot of pork, but with no yeast powder the cakes came out heavy, and sugar at 50¢ at the sutler's was too dear to sweeten them. Charles details a camp economy of dried-apple pies at 50¢ and flour cakes baked in a covered kettle, while word from the chaplain hints they will soon garrison some place near the Mississippi.

author: alexander
old: ATLANTA CAMPAIGN — NEAR MARIETTA. Sherman's flanking tactics — "comes around on the blind side.
final: Sherman "comes around on the blind side," the Johnnies told Alexander, and they "up and git" — but the letter's sharpest note is the old woman near Marietta raging not over the dead, but over a tipped barrel of ashes she wouldn't sell for two dollars and a half, while the Yankees "had a man killed and went off and wouldn't kote him off." From the skirmish line he hears the rebel cheer for Hardee come out "something very like a wail."

author: alexander
old: LUTHER WOUNDED — ball tore furrow in right side, passed through right arm above elbow. Not dangerous — two or three months recovery.
final: Luther was wounded this morning while we were after a log for the breastworks — a ball whistled close, then "a yell of agony"; Alexander ran and met him "coming back leaning upon one of the men." The ball tore a furrow in his right side and passed through his arm above the elbow — bad but not dangerous, two or three months laid up. Writing from the field near Marietta, worn "bully thin" by heat and trench work, he trades his whiskey ration for two hard crackers.

author: alexander
old: SAW ATLANTA FROM A RIDGE — spires, chimneys, smoke from furnaces, forts, rifle pits visible. Near Chattahoochee River.
final: Alexander tells his mother he likely saw the very cannon shot that killed Bishop Polk — the shell struck Polk in the breast, and had it burst, "old Johnston and Hardee would probably have shared the same fate." Days earlier, from a high ridge, the 60th Vets climbed a tree and glimpsed Atlanta itself — spires, chimneys, smoke from its furnaces, forts and rifle pits ringing the city. Until Mother's handkerchief arrived, he'd been wiping his brow with a scrap of old rebel meal bag.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF PEACHTREE CREEK (July 20, 1864). Rebs defeated with great loss — dead and wounded left on field.
final: Alexander writes from within 1¼ miles of Atlanta, his pen jumping as shells burst close: "(There goes another shot.)" "(Another shell made us jump a little just now.)" The war literally breaks into his sentences. He reports the terrific battle of the 20th — the rebs defeated with great loss, their dead and wounded left on the field, none of the Champlain boys hurt, though Captain Delaney took a bad arm wound. "How good God has been to me."

author: alexander
old: "ATLANTA EXPRESS" — battery fires shell into Atlanta every five minutes through the night. Sherman ordered batteries silent during the day, then opened at 10 P.
final: The cannonade interrupted the long letter Alexander meant to write near Atlanta on July 29, 1864: rebel batteries opened so furiously he fled to the works, where shells blew off one man's arm and killed two battery horses. By Sherman's order the guns stayed silent all day, then at 10 P.M. "the Atlanta Express" sent a shell into the city every five minutes through the night. Sent out to feint an attack while the 15th, 16th and 17th Corps shifted right, his regiment lost two men to the deception.

author: alexander
old: 23RD CORPS MOVING TO RIGHT — Schofield's movement toward Macon & Atlanta railroad. Lines within half mile of the railroad.
final: A rebel sharpshooter, nearly a mile off, sent a ball "spot" into the center of the crowd gathered for mail call -- "it made them jump a little but they did not scatter until they had got their letters." Writing from the works near Atlanta on Aug. 2, 1864, Alexander tracks Schofield's 23d Corps sweeping right to strike the Macon and Atlanta railroad. Yet what stings most is silence: "Why does not James write! I would do almost anything for him."

author: alexander
old: HOOKER LEAVES 20TH CORPS — farewell ride along the line. Pennsylvania soldier with leg shot off calls out "Good bye, General Hooker!
final: Hooker leaves the 20th Corps near Atlanta, and Alexander captures the scene that broke the men's hearts: a Pennsylvania soldier, his leg just shot off by a cannon, calls from the stretcher, "Good bye, General Hooker!" The general dismounts, removes his hat, and shakes the dying man's hand. On the right, fighting drives the enemy a mile and a half, taking a fort and battery and cutting "the only remaining road of the rebels." And still, no stamps: "ain't I a good boy?"

author: alexander
old: MOST DETAILED PEACHTREE CREEK ACCOUNT — rebels in solid columns, "seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. " Changed front three times.
final: Writing to a fellow officer, Sergeant Alexander Hubbell finally tells the Peachtree Creek story he couldn't write home: "The rebels threw their men upon us in solid columns and seemed bound to drive us into the Chattahoochee. But we were not to be driven." His regiment changed front three times — "I thought matters looked a little 'scaly' when I saw the rebs coming up in our rear" — yet was the only one in the brigade not broken.

author: james
old: EARLY'S RAID ON WASHINGTON — 153rd NY sent from Louisiana to Washington defenses. Placed in rifle pits.
final: Frederick City's hospital sits pleasantly on a hill overlooking the city, but young James writes Mother and Fannie of frustration, not glory: sent from Louisiana to Washington's defenses, dropped into rifle pits, then chasing Early through the Shenandoah while the rebels escaped with a plundered wagon train three miles long. "Our Generals marched and counter-marched without seeming to come to any determination," he writes — until a blistered foot and want of sleep dropped him from the column.

author: alexander
old: SCURVY — Alexander hospitalized near Atlanta. Surgeon says very young for it.
final: Alexander writes his mother from the 2d Division Hospital, 20th Corps, near Atlanta, struck down not by a bullet but by "genuine scurvy" — the surgeon telling him he is very young to have it. From his cot he can only hear the war: heavy firing to the right, rebels said to charge the works drunk and "repulsed each time with terrible slaughter." A McClellan man, he feels his politics turning: "I will hoist my colors soon," reckoning he'll be over 21 to cast his first vote this fall.

author: charles
old: SHERIDAN'S ARMY FORMS — 19th, 6th, and 8th Corps under Sheridan with large cavalry force near Harper's Ferry. Haven't engaged rebs yet — cavalry has fought some.
final: Sheridan's army takes shape around Harper's Ferry, but Charles writes mainly to quiet a worried mother: he is sorry she wasted $5 telegraphing about James, sent thin and with diarrhea to a hospital near Frederick. Safe in the convalescent department as a clerk, he has "flatted in considerably" on all the sugar he can eat. His counsel is hard-won: "You must call no news good news."

author: alexander
old: FALL OF ATLANTA IMMINENT — 20th Corps fallen back to Chattahoochee line. Rest of army on "grand flanking excursion" toward Macon.
final: Three of a mother's sons in three hospitals at once — and Alexander, laid up with scurvy, confesses he "did have a hearty laugh" at "your three hopeful sons being in the hospital at the one and same time." Between jokes about low diet and doctor's medicines, he relays the news: his 20th Corps has fallen back to hold the Chattahoochee line while the rest of the army swings off on a "grand flanking excursion" toward Macon. Camp rumor says the rebels have already left Atlanta.

author: alexander
old: WHEELER'S RAID — Confederate cavalry tore up railroad, preventing hospital train from reaching Nashville. Stopped at Chattanooga.
final: Wheeler's cavalry tore up the Nashville road, so Alexander's hospital train, two nights and a day out, was forced to stop at Chattanooga, where he writes his mother a tired, brief note: pretty sick yesterday, much better today, soon able to rejoin the regiment. Even from a hospital bed he frets over the Chicago convention of the 29th, waiting a day or two to learn whom the Democrats will nominate for President.

author: alexander
old: 60TH NY VETS ESCORT PAYMASTER — regiment comes through Chattanooga. Government owes Alexander $240.
final: 60th N.Y. Vets. were pulled from the front to escort the 20th Corps Paymaster down to Chattanooga — and carried five long-overdue letters to Alexander in U.S. Field Hospital No. 2, where he was fighting "this misnamed scurvy" with a daily drink of lime water. Too uncertain of his next move to draw pay with the regiment, he reckoned the government owed him $240. His politics he stated plainly: "I am a 'war man.' That's enough."

author: charles
old: THIRD BATTLE OF WINCHESTER (Sept 19, 1864) — "battle near Winchester two days since. 4 killed, 12 wounded in company.
final: James came out of the battle near Winchester two days since unhurt — Charles writes his mother in thanks, four killed and twelve wounded in their company. James, nicely recruited from the hospital, rejoined the regiment that lost 55 wounded and 10 killed; the rebs were whipped and driven to Strasburg, where they are making a stand. Charles, still with the Brigade Commissary, confesses he is "getting fat" on good living while his regiment bleeds.

author: alexander
old: THREE-YEAR ANNIVERSARY — September 21, 1861 to September 21, 1864. "Three long — long — weary years!
final: Three years to the day since he swore his oath, Alexander writes from U.S. Hospital No. 2 in Chattanooga — "three long — long — weary years!" — his first time hospitalized sick rather than wounded. He reports a strange affliction: "as soon as it is night comes I am as blind as a bat," with others around him troubled the same way. A postscript betrays his dread: morning papers carry word of a heavy fight in the Shenandoah Valley, and he is anxious to hear from the boys.

author: alexander
old: Brief note to Frances — apology for not writing. Not feeling well.
final: On his three-year anniversary in the service, Alexander Hubbell can manage only "an apology for a letter" — a few dutiful lines penned from U.S. Field Hospital No. 2 at Chattanooga on September 21, 1864.
