Too unwell to do more, he promises Fannie a long letter "before a great while" and asks only that she write often. "I only write them to let you know I have not forgotten you."

author: james
old: SHENANDOAH CAMPAIGN — Third Winchester and Fisher's Hill described from James's perspective. Pursuit — burning rebel wagons, demoralized enemy.
final: At Harrisonburg in the Shenandoah, James writes his brother Alex after two fights that drove the rebels back — wagons left burning along the night roads — then the pullback to Cedar Creek near Strasburg, burning barns as they went. He fears Alex Douglas, fallen to the rear on a march, has been "boggled by the guerrillas," and recounts a foraging boy nearly hanged as a spy who slipped free mid-battle. At 18 he votes plainly: "I go for old Abe; he is the man."

author: charles
old: $1,202 BOUNTY for one-year recruit — inflation of bounties by late 1864. SHERIDAN'S BURNING — cavalry burned barns and grist mills to Staunton.
final: Charles writes to Alexander from Harrisonburg, fresh off rejoining the regiment after being cut loose from a too-crowded commissary, and the war reaches him as ledger and labor: a Fresseville recruit drawing $1,202 bounty for one year, rations wagoned ninety miles from Harper's Ferry, cavalry burning barns and grist mills toward Stanton. "A man is no soldier unless he is lousy," he reports — war as housekeeping in a rich valley being eaten bare.

author: alexander
old: STRAW POLL ON HOSPITAL TRAIN — 37 Lincoln, 5 McClellan. Lincoln "the favored one.
final: At Chattanooga the army told Alexander "but, but, but" — a doctor's stammered refusal of the furlough he'd earned, granted instead to a man whose scurvy was "not near so bad." Writing from Hospital No. 3 in Nashville on October 10, 1864, his eyes mending and his regiment beckoning, he tallies the war's politics in miniature: on the hospital car from Chattanooga, thirty-seven men voted Lincoln, five McClellan. "Lincoln seems to be the favored one."

author: charles
old: BATTLE OF CEDAR CREEK (October 19, 1864) — one of the war's most dramatic battles. SURPRISE ATTACK — rebs got behind breastworks before they knew it.
final: At dawn near Strasburg, James woke Charles with a shout — "The Rebs are here!" — and the Battle of Cedar Creek erupted. Charles tells a soldier's story of surprise: breastworks overrun, his brigade scrambling across a ravine as bullets came thick up the hill. James took a flesh wound to the hip and walked five miles to the hospital, a bandage torn from his own drawers. 7 wounded, 2 killed in his company alone.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER FOR LINCOLN — "square and fair for Abraham Lincoln. " The McClellan devotee of April 1864 has completed his political shift.
final: Alexander writes from U.S.A. Hospital No. 3 in Nashville that he refused the oath prescribed in New York's voting law and so lost his chance to vote — yet "could I have voted I should have cast it 'square and fair' for Abraham Lincoln," adding that the majority of soldiers will vote that way. Beneath the politics runs a quieter ache: a son begging his mother to write "a long letter telling me all the news since last August."

author: james
old: JAMES'S CEDAR CREEK ACCOUNT — wounded in left thigh, walked miles to avoid capture. Complete rout of 8th Corps, surprise attack, then Union rally — "three times terribly whipped" in the Valley.
final: Wounded in the left thigh at Cedar Run, James walked several miles to keep from falling into the Johnnies' hands, then rode thirty miles in an army wagon and 120 in a freight car — "that journey was a hard one." He writes Alex from Patterson Park Hospital convinced the Rebs are finished in the Valley, "three times terribly whipped," and means to cast his first vote for Abraham Lincoln.

author: charles
old: GRANDMOTHER'S DEATH. Post-Cedar Creek camp life — drill, dress parade.
final: Grandmother's death reaches Charles in camp at Cedar Creek, where his company is down to its survivors. He hunts for news of the wounded: brother James walked to the hospital, likely a flesh wound; James Lucas lay on the ground all day before an ambulance came; Sgt. Pelkier, shot in the leg, was left in a barn for the rebels but found alive that night. "I sent my vote to Silas, voted for Lincoln. Only two votes for Lincoln in our Co."

author: charles
old: SEVEN MONTHS PAY — $108 received Dec 9. Winter quarters at Newtown — stone fireplace, chimney.
final: Charles writes from winter quarters near Newtown, Virginia, where seven months' pay finally arrives — $108 on December 9th, plus snow six inches deep and rumors of a march past Winchester to guard a railroad. The Thanksgiving turkey ration was so thin that three men in a tent traded it for four hard tacks. Asked by Frances how he looks, he draws himself plainly: mustache and chin whiskers, "quite savage," round-shouldered as ever, shaving only when a razor allows.

author: alexander
old: BATTLE OF NASHVILLE IMMINENT — Hood in front of the city. Building breastworks.
final: Hood's army has pushed to the gates of Nashville, and Alexander writes his mother from inside the fortifications, raising breastworks as skirmish fire and artillery crackle around the city. Fort Negley's heavy guns already pound the rebels close by. His confidence never wavers: "Gen. Hood will have to whistle for his supper." Yet he chafes at his posting, wanting his regiment and disgusted that "the officers drink altogether too much whiskey."

author: james
old: CHESTNUT HILL HOSPITAL — Philadelphia. Wound nearly healed.
final: At Chestnut Hill Hospital his wound has nearly healed, and James is restless to rejoin his regiment — "I feel like getting back again." He recounts the Thanksgiving feast served to the ward: turkey and gravy, oyster soup, cranberry preserves, ice cream, all gone cold because the table was too large. To a mother fretting over Alex, he insists, "You do not know how well a soldier boy can take care of himself."

author: charles
old: Practical boot transaction — bought government cavalry boots for $5. Six inches of snow. Expects to move to guard railroad. Mittens with one finger requested.
final: Charles writes from a snowbound Camp near Newtown, Virginia, to cancel a request: never mind the boots, Mother — he bought a pair of government cavalry boots last night for five dollars, when sutlers want ten to fifteen. He acknowledges fifty dollars sent on the 10th, and asks only for one-fingered mittens, the best kind. Six inches of snow, a hard west wind drifting it across the camp; the weather alone keeps them here, and soon they expect to move down to guard the railroad.

author: alexander
old: THREE DAYS BEFORE BATTLE OF NASHVILLE. Beyond pickets for firewood — "was not fired at.
final: Three days before the Battle of Nashville, with two inches of snow on the ground, Alexander goes beyond the pickets after rails for firewood and drops into the pit of an advanced picket, a colored soldier, to reconnoiter. The man tells him that could he "only les get his eye onto one of dem rebs he would fetch him sure," and Alexander agrees: "These colored soldiers fight well." He waits, heartily sick of Nashville, for Thomas to take the offensive.

author: charles
old: FALL OF SAVANNAH — brigade gave rousing cheers. Alexander lucky to miss 500-mile march.
final: Charles writes his mother from picket duty at Camp Russell near Newtown, Virginia, the year ending as it began: in the field, on guard, out of stamps. The fall of Savannah drew "rousing cheers" from the brigade, though he reckons brother Alex lucky to have missed that 500-mile march. "I hore the war is nearly over, but have not much faith that it is." He encloses twenty dollars for taxes and bonds, and one weary plea: send postage stamps, for James has none either.

author: mother
old: MOTHER'S JOY AT ALEXANDER'S SURVIVAL — feared dead at Nashville. CHAMPLAIN UNDER MILITARY RULE — 150 soldiers, cavalry stables, pickets, borders sealed against Canada (post-St.
final: Mother's letters of the 24th and 25th arrive at last — "you are among the living while my fears had numbered you with the dead," she writes Alexander, whom she'd feared killed in the battles before Nashville. Now Champlain itself stands under military rule: 150 soldiers, stables rising for a hundred horses, pickets on every bridge, the Canadian border sealed. Beneath the masquerade balls and scarlet-coated bands runs her deeper dread — no word from James since December 9.

author: charles
old: POST-WAR OCCUPATION — 153rd NY sent from Washington to Savannah for occupation duty. River obstructed with piles and forts.
final: Charles writes his mother in haste to catch the night steamer: his regiment left Washington June 5th and landed at Savannah that morning, the war over but his service not. He marvels at a river so well obstructed that piles ran nearly bank to bank past two or three forts, and recalls a swimmer swept toward the open sea before marines rowed out to him. The city "looks deserted," and his three years are up October 17th — though whether he'll be mustered out before then, he cannot say.

author: alexander
old: POST-WAR DEMOBILIZATION. Corps and division broken up.
final: Chris Greene's leg "hung by a few muscles and these they were obliged to sever with a pocket knife" — two men of the regiment cut it free, carried him from Ringgold, and he later gave each an engraved star. Alexander writes it as history, not horror, in a letter sending $350 home in coupon bonds. He confesses he sold his old watch "to buy bread to keep life in me" — the army did not always feed its sick.

author: alexander
old: 60TH NY VETS MUSTERED OUT. "The long wished for order came.
final: The long wished-for order came at last: on June 26, 1865, near Alexandria, Virginia, the Sixtieth New York Veteran Volunteers were ordered mustered out "immediately," and Alexander writes his sister Fannie to say he is coming home to Ogdensburgh to be discharged and paid off. "That's a happy day that will be, eh, Miss Fannie." Four years on, he marvels that a nation once racked "from its base to its center" now stands "free and united" — by the providence of God.

author: charles
old: POST-WAR SAVANNAH — July 4th, 1865: all-black fire company parade, "the darkeys young and old all turned out. " Cotton being hauled 160 miles to Savannah.
final: Savannah, July 13, 1865: in the first peacetime Fourth, Charles watches the city's fire companies parade, "all black but one — the darkeys young and old all turned out," while cotton rolls in from a hundred and sixty miles off. James's nighttime blindness has trailed him here; he sees fine by day but not after dark. Charles and James have expressed home one hundred and thirty dollars and wait, half-hoping, to be discharged before the tomatoes come ripe.

author: alexander
old: ALEXANDER'S LAST LETTER — THE HOMECOMING. Camp Wheeler, Ogdensburgh — the same place he enlisted in September 1861.
final: Alexander writes his shortest letter ever from Camp Wheeler in Ogdensburgh, N.Y. — waiting on a Paymaster who still hasn't come, doubting he'll make it home this week, though he is "very anxious to see you all again." He'll bring Luther down to "our house," and saves the news of "a grand reception" for the tea table. The very paper is borrowed: a printed "Soldier's Letter" poem from a boy who doesn't much like writing.

author: mother
old: POST-WAR LIFE — 1870. Five years after the war.
final: Mother's last letter is no war letter at all: "My dear boys," she writes from Champlain five years on, gently scolding an unacknowledged thirty-dollar draft, recounting a grand Thanksgiving at Uncle William's, and fretting they'll freeze unless they double their house's thickness and bank it against the northern cold. She has set seven window panes herself, and reports Uncle William's new cheese factory "better than bonds." Ordinary life, hard-won.
